#9716. A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

TTS systems evaluated on objective metrics.

Congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

#9714. Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?

The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).

The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com.

Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.

The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.

The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.

Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].

The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com.

Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.

The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.

IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.

Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.

The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.

Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.

Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.

A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.

That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.

More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.

Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.

Further reading: GangExposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.

The Qilin ransomware admin Haise’s now-deleted Telegram account, advertising the affiliate program in July 2024. Image: justpaste.it/iosba.

#9713. Egyptian and Nigerian English join the Open ASR Leaderboard

A few months ago, we added private data to the Open ASR Leaderboard: 11 splits from Appen and DataOceanAI covering scripted and conversational speech from five accents (blog). The community response was great, with many highlighting the importance of held-out sets for trustworthy evaluations. Since then, we added one more private split for Indian-accented English with Voice Arena (blog).

We’re excited to announce a new collaboration with Liva AI to add even more private data with two new accents: Egyptian 🇪🇬 and Nigerian 🇳🇬.

This is part of our continued effort to improve representation in ASR evals (more accents and more languages) and to improve trust (new private data to minimize benchmaxxing, and new data providers). We’re excited to see the community continuing to push ASR performance for the world 🤗

With these new accents, we can now present a richer breakdown of accents, based on Kachru’s Three Circles (kudos to Hume AI for this idea in their leaderboard). The Open ASR Leaderboard will now report:

As more accents join, we’ll split the Outer and Expanding Circles.

Liva AI collects multimodal interaction data through consumer products used by real people. Because Liva owns both the collection environment and distribution, it can design products around specific model gaps across domains, industries, languages, modalities, and interaction types. This gives it access to natural, high-context behavior that emerges through real product use, rather than artificially elicited or task-based interactions.

#9712. Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.

Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization. Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.

Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance. Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.

Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.

In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers.

In a standard MoE, each layer has EEE experts, and each input token xxx is routed independently to KKK such experts ( K=8 K = 8 K=8 is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights gk(x)g_{k}(x)gk​(x) for each expert kkk, wherein the KKK experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, T(x)⊂{1,..,E}T(x) \subset\{1,..,E\}T(x)⊂{1,..,E}. The output of the layer is then ∑k∈T(x)gk(x)fk(x)\sum\limits_{k\in T(x)}g_{k}(x)f_{k}(x)k∈T(x)∑​gk​(x)fk​(x), where fk(x)f_{k}(x)fk​(x) is the output of expert kkk for token xxx.

Left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts.

Importantly, experts in the selected set T(x)T(x)T(x) are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed before in the literature, as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout.

This means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly important, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately.

This effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous.

(See Appendix A in our corresponding paper for the full derivation of the HOPE objective)

When we delete a set of PPP experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts T(x)T(x)T(x) (for any token xxx) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error. Our goal is to find the prune-set PPP (of some predefined pruning budget ∣P∣\vert P\vert∣P∣) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens xxx from our calibration set).

Unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over PPP directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set PPP itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate ZZZ, which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error:

Z=[∑j∈P∩T(x)gj(x)∥fj(x)∥2]2≥true errorZ = \bigl[\sum\limits_{j \in P\cap T(x)} g_{j}(x)\Vert f_j(x)\Vert_{2}\bigr]^{2} \geq \text{true error}Z=[j∈P∩T(x)∑​gj​(x)∥fj​(x)∥2​]2≥true error

Because ZZZ is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms gi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​ between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard.

To find the optimal prune-set, HOPE minimizes E[Z]\mathbb{E}[Z]E[Z] over the calibration set, which can be reformulated as the following quadratic program:

P∗=arg min⁡p  p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,∑k=1Epk=∣P∣P^{*} = \argmin_{p}\; p^{\top}Fp \quad \text{s.t.} \quad p \in \{0,1\}^{E}, \sum\limits_{k=1}^{E}p_{k} = \vert P\vertP∗=pargmin​p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,k=1∑E​pk​=∣P∣

where F∈RE×EF\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E}F∈RE×E is defined as:

Fi,j=1∣Xi,j∣∑x∈Xi,jgi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2whereXi,j={x:i,j∈T(x)}F_{i,j} = \frac{1}{\vert \mathcal{X}_{i,j}\vert} \sum\limits_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i,j}} g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}\quad\text{where}\quad \mathcal{X}_{i,j} = \{x: i,j \in T(x)\}Fi,j​=∣Xi,j​∣1​x∈Xi,j​∑​gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​whereXi,j​={x:i,j∈T(x)}

This F-matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, and the optimal prune-set is obtained by solving the resulting quadratic program (QP) with a continuous relaxation (then rounding to binary solutions). Each entry Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts iii and jjj, across tokens where both are co-activated. Whereas the diagonal Fk,kF_{k,k}Fk,k​ measures individual expert importance, the off-diagonal entries ( Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ for i≠ji\neq ji=j) measure pairwise cooperative contribution.

What does FFF look like in practice? It shows the structure of expert cooperation, which depends on layer:

Visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM-4.5-Air (128 experts per layer, 106B parameters total) at three representative layers (early, middle, late). Experts have been clustered to reveal block structure. Bright blocks along the diagonal indicate groups of experts with strong pairwise interaction scores.

In terms of practical cost, HOPE requires the same calibration pass as any other expert-pruning method (one forward pass over calibration data). The only addition is solving the quadratic program, which is non-convex, but can be solved efficiently via a standard QP solver (1–2 seconds each layer). The total additional overhead is negligible compared to first-order methods, as the time for calibration dominates.

Notably, HOPE has a strong connection to Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP), a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of FFF recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ρ=0.988\rho = 0.988ρ=0.988). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the FFF-matrix.

We evaluated HOPE as an expert pruning method using 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, and GLM-4.5-Air), with 2 calibration datasets (Evol-CodeAlpaca and SWE-Bench Verified trajectories). We used the Tulu3 suite and SWE-Bench Pro (agentic coding) to test the resulting pruned models, comparing HOPE to 4 first-order baselines (REAP, MAN, EAN, and Frequency) across pruning rates spanning from 10% to 50%.

HOPE achieves the best overall rank across conditions and dominates at aggressive pruning rates. Left: average rank (lower = better) across all models, calibration sets, and benchmarks. Right: SWE-Bench Pro performance on Qwen3.5-35B.

Across all conditions, HOPE achieved the best average rank (2.07 out of 5 methods), with the highest rate of top-1 finishes (39% of conditions) and top-2 finishes (67%). In a head-to-head comparison, HOPE beats every other baseline in the majority of conditions.

As expected, HOPE's advantage grows at higher pruning rates. As more experts are removed, more cooperative links are broken, and the off-diagonal terms of FFF become more important. At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves to 1.58 (vs. 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP). This is also the most deployment-relevant setting, where memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning, and more tool calls.

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro, an agentic coding benchmark where models must solve real GitHub issues autonomously. These problems involve compositionally diverse tasks (e.g. coding, tool calls, reasoning, etc.) over many turns and likely exercise diverse expert combinations—exactly the regime where preserving cooperative structure matters most. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE achieved 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned model's 41.8 (while REAP dropped to 36.2, a 13% regression).

Notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and has been observed across pruning methods. Furthermore, our experiments showed that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.

Average strength of cooperation (measured by F-matrix value) with retained experts, split by experts on which HOPE and REAP disagree.

HOPE's advantage stems from optimizing over the entire interaction matrix FFF. To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. The gains in benchmark performance (shown above) validate that this trade-off is advantageous.

We created a basic package to run HOPE. It has three steps: 1) calibrate; 2) solve; 3) prune. Our package has been tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and GLM-4.5.

The calibration step runs a single forward pass over calibration data, whether it be agentic rollouts or single-turn traces. This uses HuggingFace transformers to hook into the forward pass of each individual MoE layer. For each token, this records which experts are selected, their gate weights, output norms, and pairwise co-activation statistics. The output of this step is the F-matrix, stored in an HDF5 file.

This command materializes the F-matrix and solves the binary quadratic program via a continuous relaxation. This takes a few seconds per layer, and the output is a JSON file which contains the prune-set. This is technically the final output of the HOPE algorithm.

To complete the pipeline, we run this command to actually create the smaller model checkpoint from the prune-set. The pruned model is a standard HuggingFace checkpoint which is smaller on disk and in memory (no changes to vLLM or SGLang model definitions needed).

We also released a more compact Python API:

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced at higher pruning rates (40–50%). At lower pruning rates (10–20%), first-order methods like REAP and MAN are sometimes competitive, and HOPE's advantage shrinks. Additionally, as with most expert-pruning algorithms, HOPE prunes each layer independently and does not account for cross-layer interactions. In our paper, we presented a theoretical framework for cross-layer HOPE, but the results remain preliminary. Finally, HOPE captures pairwise interactions, but even higher-order interactions (triplets and beyond) could provide additional signal, although they are combinatorially difficult to estimate.

For more information, see our corresponding paper and codebase.

To see how HOPE can be applied to next-generation hybrid architectures, see our corresponding repository.

#9711. Building a Multi-Agent Website Launch Validator With OpenMinion

Founder of Design Master Solutions. I build websites, apps and AI agents for small businesses in the US and Brazil.

Founder of Design Master Solutions. I build websites, apps and AI agents for small businesses in the US and Brazil.

Founder of Design Master Solutions. I build websites, apps and AI agents for small businesses in the US and Brazil.

I run a small web agency. We build and host websites for small businesses in the US and Brazil, and every launch has the same floor: a title and a description, a canonical URL, Open Graph tags, JSON-LD, icons, a sitemap, a 404 page that really returns 404, an llms.txt, and a robots.txt that does not lock AI search crawlers out. For years we checked that list by hand, one tab per item.

For Cortensor Hackathon 5, I turned the checklist into an agent called Go-Live Gate, built on OpenMinion 0.1, the agent SDK from the Cortensor ecosystem. It answers one question: is this site ready, ready with warnings, or blocked? The code is MIT-licensed at github.com/DesignMaster-Solutions/golive-gate and there is a 2-minute demo at youtu.be/tVH-x62QV3I.

This post is about the one design decision that made it trustworthy, and about what it looks like to run an agent on open, swappable inference instead of one vendor's API.

The tempting version of this agent is one prompt: "here is a URL, tell me if it is ready". That version hallucinates. It will tell you a sitemap exists because sites usually have one.

So Go-Live Gate is split in three agents with different powers:

Every run writes facts.json next to report.md. A reviewer can open both and check the model's verdict against what the tools actually saw. That file is the whole point: the agent is only as honest as the layer under it, and that layer has its own offline tests against a local HTTP server.

When the facts live in code and the model only reasons over them, the model becomes replaceable. That is what makes open inference practical for a business tool.

OpenMinion talks to any OpenAI-compatible provider. Our recorded runs used a free open-weight model (nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free through OpenRouter); the same project is set up for the Cortensor Portal with one command (setup --provider cortensor-portal). I did not have to rewrite prompts or tools to switch. The judge's output is validated by a schema either way, so a weaker or slower node fails loudly instead of quietly writing a wrong verdict.

If you are building on a decentralized inference network, you cannot assume the same model, the same latency or the same token limits on every call. Designing the agent so that the model is the least trusted part is how you get repeatable results anyway.

The hackathon asked for building blocks tested and lessons learned, and these were the useful ones:

And one bug was mine. The first live run flagged a 697-character title on a client site whose real title is 63 characters. My parser was concatenating the elements inside inline SVG icons. The agent repeated what the tool reported, which is exactly why the facts layer has regression tests and the model does not get the last word.</p> <p>On capegraniteconnection.com, a site we built, the gate returned ready with 11 checks: title 63 characters, description 149, canonical present, all four Open Graph tags, 12 JSON-LD types including LocalBusiness and FAQPage, en-US, both icons, no AI crawler blocked, a sitemap with 44 URLs, a 3,902-byte llms.txt, and a real 404. On a free model the investigator took 232 seconds and the judge 355. Slow, but it runs unattended before every launch, and it is cheaper than the hour of tabs it replaces.</p> <p>The lesson I would carry to any agent on open infrastructure: let code collect the facts, let the model reason over them, put a schema on the answer and a human in front of anything that writes. Then the model can come from anywhere.</p> <p>Founder of Design Master Solutions. I build websites, apps and AI agents for small businesses in the US and Brazil.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://hackernoon.com/building-a-multi-agent-website-launch-validator-with-openminion?source=rss" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9710"> <h2>#9710. Decision Models in Hugging Face</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://huggingface.co/blog/assets/decision/thumbnail.png" alt="Decision Models in Hugging Face" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.</p> <p>Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:</p> <p>"I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today."</p> <p>The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.</p> <p>We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.</p> <p>But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?</p> <p>This is the key idea behind decision models.</p> <p>A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.</p> <p>TypeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a System One model. The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).</p> <p>The community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models)</p> <p>For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:</p> <p>We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.</p> <p>However, there are a few problems with this approach.</p> <p>Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.</p> <p>Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:</p> <p>A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.</p> <p>The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.</p> <p>If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.</p> <p>Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.</p> <p>Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.</p> <p>One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.</p> <p>This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.</p> <p>Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).</p> <p>More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.</p> <p>The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.</p> <p>A decision model request has the following two components:</p> <p>The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.</p> <p>Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:</p> <p>Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.</p> <p>Which department should handle this customer request?</p> <p>The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.</p> <p>The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits z1,…,zKz_1,\ldots,z_Kz1​,…,zK​, (with KKK classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:</p> <p>pi=exp⁡(zi)∑j=1Kexp⁡(zj) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} pi​=∑j=1K​exp(zj​)exp(zi​)​</p> <p>∑i=1Kpi=1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i=1∑K​pi​=1.</p> <p>The model chooses the option with the largest probability:</p> <p>y^=arg⁡max⁡ipi \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y^​=argimax​pi​</p> <p>In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.</p> <p>Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?</p> <p>The model again produces a probability distribution:</p> <p>Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index.</p> <p>For a random variable XXX representing the level, the expectation is:</p> <p>E[X]=∑i=0K−1ipi \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E[X]=i=0∑K−1​ipi​</p> <p>E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7</p> <p>This does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7.</p> <p>The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question.</p> <p>Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli).</p> <p>Y∼Bernoulli⁡(p) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y∼Bernoulli(p)</p> <p>P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p. P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p.</p> <p>it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No.</p> <p>The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it.</p> <p>So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score.</p> <p>The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that.</p> <p>For a Choice with KKK options, the confidence is:</p> <p>pmax⁡−1K1−1K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1−K1​pmax​−K1​​</p> <p>where pmax⁡p_{\max}pmax​ is the largest predicted probability.</p> <p>In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.998:</p> <p>C=3(0.998)−12=0.997 C=\frac{3(0.998)-1}{2}=0.997 C=23(0.998)−1​=0.997</p> <p>Notice that the winning probability is 0.998, but the reported confidence is 0.997. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558.</p> <p>Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.</p> <p>Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:</p> <p>The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces.</p> <p>Transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline, AutoModelForDecision, and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models.</p> <p>One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so:</p> <p>Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint.</p> <p>We can start a local server using the serving dependencies:</p> <p>Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request:</p> <p>The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities.</p> <p>An interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a new model.</p> <p>llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API.</p> <p>For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub:</p> <p>We can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone. With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request.</p> <p>The useful property is interface compatibility.</p> <p>Hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture.</p> <p>For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones.</p> <p>Once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API.</p> <p>Below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it shows the parts that matter:</p> <p>First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL (huggingface/trl#8040), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open.</p> <p>If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head.</p> <p>Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.</p> <p>Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.</p> <p>Great write-up. The step the post leaves to the application, turning noul: 0.83 into an action, is where things get hard in production. It's usually a threshold (if p > 0.9), and it quietly goes stale: raw probabilities are rarely calibrated, the right cut-off depends on what a mistake costs, and the outcome that says whether the decision was right (a chargeback, a reassigned ticket) arrives days or months later.</p> <p>I'm building an open-source, self-hosted tool for that loop: trimset. It sits in front of any /v1/systemone server (so transformers serve or llama.cpp) with a one-line URL change. It logs every decision and joins the real outcome when it arrives. It calibrates per question and model, then compiles thresholds and an escalation band with a stated guarantee ("false passes ≤ 2% with 95% confidence"), which your app applies locally. It's pre-alpha; drift and silent-upgrade alerts come next.</p> <p>Live demo on recorded data, threshold simulator included: https://demo.trimset.dev/#/questions/refund_fraud/simulator</p> <p>For anyone running decision models in production: how do you pick your cut-offs today?</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://huggingface.co/blog/decision" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9709"> <h2>#9709. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.</span></p><h3 id="1278208"><a href="https://partner.canva.com/c/3290703/1278208/10068"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Canva Sign Up </span></a></h3> <img border="0" height="0" src="https://imp.pxf.io/i/3290703/1278208/10068" width="0" /><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Designing with Canva</span></h3><div><div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"><a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEgM7YZbpEWXuX7McOKgqVQgrWlabYMSo3a4U9zch0MoomYWl4xBhgZrVjiZKA9hMBEkEL-5IkdFFkw7rotiewBPKDjunpoe6eBXwmG_rk7Ntkw0l4h-bdBMY5LJtS_QFWWkauczX7J4wI5aMMPmHD3nKre-xTEzdLvVVgx5IC5lEAbNpIgSB6kEMRO-iw=s1280" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><img alt="canva" border="0" height="436" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEgM7YZbpEWXuX7McOKgqVQgrWlabYMSo3a4U9zch0MoomYWl4xBhgZrVjiZKA9hMBEkEL-5IkdFFkw7rotiewBPKDjunpoe6eBXwmG_rk7Ntkw0l4h-bdBMY5LJtS_QFWWkauczX7J4wI5aMMPmHD3nKre-xTEzdLvVVgx5IC5lEAbNpIgSB6kEMRO-iw=w640-h436" title="canva" width="640" /></span></a></div><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><br /><span><br /></span></span></div><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.</span></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Templates</span></h3><div><div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"><a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEimJ6jOhTnmaFvrB_VTjmU4f5D4AqXjy65hqYROJW4_z_-EN0phhYBAoCpgD5iq2ICEF19CE6CS1o41joiTQDR12n-trPkotc4gGOggwyf2qpLR5G8pHkXd6DszzjsvJ_OtRZFE5vAUw81Gvv3kr_gdmA_JhhBjSpMDkj1lBWJb1uJeVbPsqwUKgLgMoQ=s1280" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><img alt="canva templates" border="0" height="442" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEimJ6jOhTnmaFvrB_VTjmU4f5D4AqXjy65hqYROJW4_z_-EN0phhYBAoCpgD5iq2ICEF19CE6CS1o41joiTQDR12n-trPkotc4gGOggwyf2qpLR5G8pHkXd6DszzjsvJ_OtRZFE5vAUw81Gvv3kr_gdmA_JhhBjSpMDkj1lBWJb1uJeVbPsqwUKgLgMoQ=w640-h442" title="canva templates" width="640" /></span></a></div><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><br /><span><br /></span></span></div><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.</span></p> <div id="atContainer-291a91492f7bcf13f252654de362127b"></div> <span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><br /> <span> Canva has a lot to choose from, so start with a specific search.if you want to create business card just search for it and you will see alot of templates to choose from</span></span><p></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Elements</span></h3><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.</span></p><p></p><div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"><a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEiMPph53bq8js4qlIL55ERQwzAxyL406RSoDJ10bhJ8iO_mlKHtuaQBKAVr4iLEbJh4xEQW7QOfDXOqV1sbYv3qRdMssBchVFWWFqfANHdeX0461ZaBsX_bsLwrB-ad4OyJFfAu03Jyok1fCMvpR5IiBnFjOxVIYbP9AQe7Zs6NIHKwspoD8hl3unL3Dw=s1280" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><img alt="canva elements" border="0" height="442" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEiMPph53bq8js4qlIL55ERQwzAxyL406RSoDJ10bhJ8iO_mlKHtuaQBKAVr4iLEbJh4xEQW7QOfDXOqV1sbYv3qRdMssBchVFWWFqfANHdeX0461ZaBsX_bsLwrB-ad4OyJFfAu03Jyok1fCMvpR5IiBnFjOxVIYbP9AQe7Zs6NIHKwspoD8hl3unL3Dw=w640-h442" title="canva elements" width="640" /></span></a></div><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><br /></span><p></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:</span></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Photos</span></h3><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.</span></p><p></p><div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"><a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEhKT6RizHZUEKqQQAV8rZZUDBHG_7b8oD-2jNuEUsf4q2RYa7Nx_QDTVSL7vBWvdi8NWBEyV2sKMtE4MtIFgc5O6ggDlunJMNa8ilfAFIWG3xMWQiqY0BKZFHRxn0151lEbOj-6QykEt28OY8e_0F_WyloPPKbiXLH-h68degeJZzyHZddkSO0Ge-zamA=s1280" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><img alt="canva photos" border="0" height="442" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEhKT6RizHZUEKqQQAV8rZZUDBHG_7b8oD-2jNuEUsf4q2RYa7Nx_QDTVSL7vBWvdi8NWBEyV2sKMtE4MtIFgc5O6ggDlunJMNa8ilfAFIWG3xMWQiqY0BKZFHRxn0151lEbOj-6QykEt28OY8e_0F_WyloPPKbiXLH-h68degeJZzyHZddkSO0Ge-zamA=w640-h442" title="canva photos" width="640" /></span></a></div><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><br /></span><p></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"> When you subscribe to Canva Pro, you get access to a number of premium features, including the Background Remover. This feature allows you to remove the background from any stock photo in  library or any image you upload.</span></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Text</span></h3><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows). </span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Canva Pro subscribers can choose from a large library of fonts on the Brand Kit or the Styles tab. Enterprise-level controls ensure that visual content remains on-brand, no matter how many people are working on it.</span></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Audio</span></h3><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.</span></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Video</span></h3><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab. </span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.</span></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Backgrounds</span></h3><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.</span></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Styles</span></h3><div><div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"><a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEhBQW4BOkq3UutI4TFJiQlwAkDWDeE_48rdkRxCrVrRMkhw6cDGtZKFruHN-Q54dF9446S6j9Wp-9n914SAde1veZqvCo8ATKX2UuSx-TMYq--zNtB2wkFXdtAOS4q6_1EBVCVz8kfJfo2HT2CA-ModbPaq3a86gMezGir-Vqmvz61ic-tJMfxNmblZMA=s1280" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><img border="0" height="440" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEhBQW4BOkq3UutI4TFJiQlwAkDWDeE_48rdkRxCrVrRMkhw6cDGtZKFruHN-Q54dF9446S6j9Wp-9n914SAde1veZqvCo8ATKX2UuSx-TMYq--zNtB2wkFXdtAOS4q6_1EBVCVz8kfJfo2HT2CA-ModbPaq3a86gMezGir-Vqmvz61ic-tJMfxNmblZMA=w640-h440" width="640" /></span></a></div><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><br /></span></div><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.</span></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Logos</span></h3><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.</span></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Publishing with Canva</span></h3><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Canva Pro subscribers can create multiple post formats from one design. For example, you can start by designing an Instagram post, and Canva's Magic Resizer can resize it for other networks, Stories, Reels, and other formats.</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Canva Pro subscribers can also use Canva’s Content Planner to post content on eight different accounts on Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack, and Tumblr.</span></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Canva Team</span></h3><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.</span></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Canva Print</span></h3><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts. </span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.</span></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Canva Apps</span></h3><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.</span></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Canva Pros and Cons</span></h3><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Pros:</span></h3><p></p><ul style="text-align: left;"><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">A user-friendly interface</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Canva is a great tool for people who want to create professional graphics but don’t have graphic design skills.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Hundreds of templates, so you'll never have to start from scratch.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Wide variety of templates to fit multiple uses</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Branding kits to keep your team consistent with the brand colors and fonts</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Creating visual content on the go</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">You can find royalty free images, audio, and video without having to subscribe to another service.</span></li></ul><p></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Cons:</span></h3><p></p><ul style="text-align: left;"><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Some professional templates are available for Pro user only</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Advanced photo editing features like blurring or erasing a specific area are missing.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Some elements that fall outside of a design are tricky to retrieve.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Features (like Canva presentations) could use some improvement.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">If you are a regular user of Adobe products, you might find Canva's features limited.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Prefers to work with vectors. Especially logos.</span></li><li><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Expensive enterprise pricing</span></li></ul><p></p><h3 style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">Conclusion</span></h3><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;">In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. If you have any queries let me know in the comments section.</span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><br /></span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><br /></span></p><p><span style="font-family: Comfortaa;"><br /></span></p><p><br /></p></p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://techncruncher.blogspot.com/2022/02/canva-review-2022-details-pricing.html" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9708"> <h2>#9708.
