Pay for Hugging Face Hub with your Google Cloud Account</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://huggingface.co/blog/assets/hub-gcp-marketplace/thumbnail.jpg" alt="Pay for Hugging Face Hub with your Google Cloud Account" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>You can now link your Hugging Face organization to your Google Cloud account, so that your Hugging Face usage shows up on your Google Cloud bill instead of being charged to a credit card. Get started on the Google Cloud Marketplace.</p> <p>Hugging Face is where teams find, build and run open models: from hosting private models and datasets, to running GPU workloads with Jobs, deploying models with Inference Endpoints, calling thousands of models through Inference Providers, or hosting demos on GPU Spaces.</p> <p>If your company already runs on Google Cloud, adding a new vendor and a corporate credit card just to use these services can slow things down. By linking your organization through the Google Cloud Marketplace:</p> <p>If you're an admin of your Hugging Face organization, here's how to set it up, step by step.</p> <p>Once the order is placed, Google Cloud asks you to finish setting up your account with Hugging Face. Click on "Sign up with Hugging Face" to be redirected to Hugging Face.</p> <p>You are now on Hugging Face, where you can select the organization you want to link to your Google Cloud account. Only organizations where you are an admin are listed. Select it and confirm.</p> <p>You are then redirected to the billing settings of your organization. The payment method section now shows the linked Google Cloud account, with a pending status.</p> <p>Every cloud marketplace subscription is reviewed by the Hugging Face team before paid usage starts being billed through it. While the subscription is pending, usage keeps being billed to the organization's existing payment method, if any.</p> <p>Once your subscription is approved, you will receive an email confirming that your Google Cloud account and Hugging Face organization are linked. Organizations that already have a credit card on file switch to cloud marketplace billing at the start of their next billing period. Organizations on the free tier with no credit card on file usually switch immediately, so their paid usage is billed through the cloud marketplace right away.</p> <p>To confirm it, open the billing settings of your organization: the Google Cloud account is now shown as the organization's active payment method.</p> <p>Your organization is now billed through your Google Cloud account. All members of your organization can use Hugging Face compute services, and the usage will show up on your Google Cloud bill.</p> <p>Thanks for reading! You can find more details in the billing documentation. If you have any questions, please contact us at billing@huggingface.co.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://huggingface.co/blog/hub-gcp-marketplace" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9706"> <h2>#9706. Comparing Six AI Video APIs by Cost, Concurrency, and Reliability</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://hackernoon.imgix.net/images/slT3HCgc9CZ4HGESXdHgPgAICaj1-wn83dym.jpeg" alt="Comparing Six AI Video APIs by Cost, Concurrency, and Reliability" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Business Developement Manager with a demonstrated history of working in the public relations and communication.</p> <p>Business Developement Manager with a demonstrated history of working in the public relations and communication.</p> <p>Business Developement Manager with a demonstrated history of working in the public relations and communication.</p> <p>Most AI video work still starts in a browser tab: type a prompt, wait, download. That breaks down once a team needs 200 product clips a week, a video step inside an app, or an agent that renders drafts overnight. Video APIs move generation into code. In this article, we: how the requests work, a short working example, what matters once real traffic arrives, six APIs side by side, and the automation layer on top.</p> <p>A video takes anywhere from under a minute to a few minutes to render, so no provider keeps an HTTP connection open until the file is ready. Every major video API follows the same three-part pattern.</p> <p>The names change from provider to provider. fal calls them requests, Replicate calls them predictions, and Runway calls them tasks. The shape stays the same.</p> <p>The example below uses the Higgsfield API and Seedance 2.5. The same submit, poll, and download loop works with any provider. Only the URL, auth header, and field names change.</p> <p>Step 1: Set your credentials. Create an API key in the console and export the key ID and secret.</p> <p>Step 2: Submit the job. The idempotency key lets you resend the same request after a timeout without paying twice.</p> <p>A demo needs one successful call. A production pipeline has to survive timeouts, rate limits, moderation rejections, and bills that grow with every retry. Four areas decide how much work that takes.</p> <p>Every provider caps parallel jobs. Higgsfield allows 20 concurrent requests, fal allows 2 to 40 on self-serve accounts, Runway allows 1 to 20 depending on usage tier, and MiniMax allows 30 in-flight H3 jobs. Put your own job queue in front of the API, such as a database table or a Redis list, so a batch of 500 renders waits its turn instead of failing.</p> <p>Retry network errors and 5xx responses with exponential backoff. Never retry 4xx validation errors, since the same input will fail again. Send an idempotency key with each submission so a resent POST does not start a second paid job. Treat webhooks as at-least-once: Higgsfield, fal, and Replicate can all deliver duplicates, so deduplicate by request ID. Keep a polling fallback in case a webhook never arrives.</p> <p>Failure rules differ more than prices do.</p> <p>Validate inputs before you submit. A broken image URL or an unsupported duration is the cheapest bug to catch.</p> <p>No single model wins every shot. Kling 4.0 handles long takes, Seedance 2.5 handles reference-driven scenes, and MiniMax H3 delivers 2K at a low rate. Calling each vendor directly means separate keys, balances, rate limits, and response formats. Platforms such as Higgsfield, fal, Replicate, and Runway Dev put multiple models behind one key and one balance, so switching models means changing one model ID. The trade-off is dependence on the platform’s pricing and model coverage.</p> <p>Prices are list rates per second of 720p video (768p on MiniMax), checked in late October and early November 2026. Promotions are excluded.</p> <p>50+ video and image models, incl. Kling 4.0, Seedance 2.5, MiniMax H3, Wan 3.0</p> <p>Wan 3.0 from $0.020/s; Kling 4.0 from $0.110/s</p> <p>Gen-4.5 and Aleph, plus Kling 4.0, Seedance 2.5, Gemini Omni</p> <p>Google shut down the three Veo 3.1 preview models in the Gemini API (veo-3.1-generate-preview, veo-3.1-fast-generate-preview, and veo-3.1-lite-generate-preview) on October 22, 2026, and points developers to Gemini Omni Flash instead. The generally available Veo 3.1 models remain on Google Cloud’s Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.</p> <p>Pick Higgsfield when you want top models plus production tools like consistent characters and camera control behind one key, or fal for a broad open catalog. Replicate fits teams that also deploy custom models. Runway Dev makes sense when Gen-4.5 and Aleph editing sit at the center of the pipeline. The Gemini API suits chat-style edits on Google's own model, and MiniMax wins when 2K output at a low per-second rate matters most.</p> <p>A cron job or a cloud scheduler, such as GitHub Actions, Google Cloud Scheduler, or AWS EventBridge, can read tomorrow's briefs from a sheet or database, submit one job per row, and write the finished URLs back. Pair it with webhooks so the scheduler never sits idle polling.</p> <p>Both connect to any video API through a generic HTTP step, with no custom node required. In n8n, a typical flow runs Schedule Trigger, then HTTP Request to submit, then a Wait node set to resume on a webhook call, then a download and upload to Google Drive or S3. Pass $execution.resumeUrl as the provider's webhook URL so the workflow wakes up when the video is ready. In Make, one scheduled scenario submits jobs through the HTTP module, and a second scenario that starts from a Custom webhook receives results and files them.</p> <p>The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets an AI assistant call outside tools directly. Higgsfield's MCP server connects to Claude, ChatGPT, Claude Code, and other MCP-compatible clients, and gives the agent 30+ image and video models with no API key. A marketer can ask the assistant to make three 9:16 hook variants of a product shot and get the files back without writing code. Agents work best on drafts and one-off requests. Scheduled pipelines still handle volume better.</p> <p>Which AI video API is the cheapest? Per second of output, Wan 3.0 on Higgsfield starts at $0.020, MiniMax H3 runs $0.08 at 768p, and Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash costs about $0.10 at 720p. Count retries too: a cheap model that needs four takes costs more than a pricier one that lands in one.</p> <p>Do I need webhooks, or is polling enough? Polling every 5 to 10 seconds works at low volume. As job counts grow, webhooks cut wasted requests. Keep polling as a fallback either way.</p> <p>How long do providers keep generated videos? Not long. Replicate deletes API outputs after one hour by default, and Higgsfield keeps them at least seven days. Copy each file to your own storage as soon as the job completes.</p> <p>Can I spend web app credits through the API? Usually not. Higgsfield and Runway both bill API usage from a separate prepaid balance, apart from app subscriptions.</p> <p>This article was published under HackerNoon's Business Blogging program.</p> <p>Anyone Can Copy Your Crypto App. Can They Copy Your Business?</p> <p>Business Developement Manager with a demonstrated history of working in the public relations and communication.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://hackernoon.com/comparing-six-ai-video-apis-by-cost-concurrency-and-reliability?source=rss" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9705"> <h2>#9705. Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://huggingface.co/blog/assets/train-sentence-transformers/st-hf-thumbnail.png" alt="Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up quickly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors!</p> <p>Token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget.</p> <p>In this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4, my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how.</p> <p>This post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study, which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example.</p> <p>Pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below.</p> <p>A single-vector embedding model compresses an entire document into one vector. Multi-vector models such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document.</p> <p>For example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together:</p> <p>MaxSim⁡(Q,D)=∑q∈Qmax⁡d∈Dq⊤d \operatorname{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q^\top d MaxSim(Q,D)=q∈Q∑​d∈Dmax​q⊤d</p> <p>Even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by Fast-PLAID, storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. At 4 bits per residual coordinate, 200 vectors of 128 dimensions require 12.8 KB of quantized residuals per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that to 3.2 GB, at the same dimensionality and precision.</p> <p>The useful observation is that many document vectors can be similar. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together.</p> <p>HierarchicalTokenPooling groups similar token embeddings using Ward hierarchical clustering. Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors.</p> <p>These merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring.</p> <p>You can make compression proportional to document length:</p> <p>With pool_factor=4, documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged.</p> <p>HierarchicalTokenPooling offers three alternative controls:</p> <p>This distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4, a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold, the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved.</p> <p>Adaptive pooling uses a shared distance threshold to merge similar embeddings more aggressively while preserving more vectors for documents with distinct content. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective.</p> <p>Rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. Given a representative sample of your corpus in calibration_documents:</p> <p>Calibration only needs document embeddings and returns a threshold you can reuse when indexing. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus.</p> <p>Pooling can already be useful on an ordinary multi-vector model. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. The original training objective never required the model to work with these compressed representations. But, you can teach it to do exactly that.</p> <p>If you've used Matryoshka embeddings, the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors.</p> <p>For my example, each training batch contributes two losses:</p> <p>L=12Lunpooled+12Lpooled \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{unpooled}} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pooled}} L=21​Lunpooled​+21​Lpooled​</p> <p>The first term teaches the model to retrieve with its full representations. The second teaches it to arrange its token embeddings so that useful matches survive pooling. Both objectives update the same encoder, giving it feedback about retrieval before and after compression.</p> <p>Ward clustering makes discrete decisions about which tokens belong together. During training, HierarchicalTokenPooling uses a straight-through estimator to pass gradients from pooled vectors back to their member tokens, without differentiating the cluster assignments. The encoder can then learn from retrieval errors made with its pooled representations.</p> <p>MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss wraps an existing multi-vector retrieval loss and applies it using your chosen poolers:</p> <p>CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss supplies the retrieval objective. It teaches each query to score its relevant document above the negative documents in the batch. By default, it uses model.similarity, using the model's similarity setting (MaxSim in this example) and kernel settings. A model configured with similarity_fn_name="meanmaxsim" would also use MeanMaxSim during training.</p> <p>Gradient caching allows the encoder to process small mini-batches while retaining a larger set of in-batch negatives. My training script uses mini-batches of 64 with a training batch size of 256.</p> <p>MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss adds the compression objective. Here, None means that one variant uses the original embeddings, while pooling supplies the factor-4 variant. The two weights average their losses. Pooling variants reuse the computed token embeddings, so each additional pooler adds clustering and scoring work without requiring a separate encoder pass for that variant.</p> <p>The poolers can also be custom BaseTokenPooling implementations that preserve gradients through their input embeddings. You can adapt the training objective to the representation you want to deploy.</p> <p>Replace the factor-4 pooler with your chosen deployment configuration, or include several poolers and choose weights for their losses.</p> <p>The complete training script includes the dataset, trainer, validation loss, and small retrieval evaluations during training. From a checkout of the repository, run both variants locally with uv:</p> <p>The script declares its training and kernel dependencies, so uv installs them for you. Compatible kernels are enabled automatically.</p> <p>You can also train on a cloud GPU with Hugging Face Jobs. Install the CLI and log in with a token that can run Jobs and upload models:</p> <p>This runs the pooling-aware variant on an A10G GPU with a four-hour time limit. Passing HF_TOKEN as a secret lets the script upload the trained model to your Hub account when training finishes. To run the ordinary-loss baseline as well, repeat the command with --baseline after the script URL.</p> <p>You can accelerate MaxSim scoring, Ward clustering, and supported backbone operations with kernels. Install the training and kernel dependencies:</p> <p>In the training example above, replace the model and pooler initialization before constructing the loss:</p> <p>Hierarchical poolers inherit the model's kernel settings by default, so you only need to enable kernels on the model.</p> <p>Sentence Transformers selects compatible kernels for your setup and uses the existing implementation wherever a replacement isn't available. For example, the default MaxSim kernel scores queries against documents without building the full token similarity matrix in memory, but it does require CUDA and Triton.</p> <p>The default Ward clustering kernel considerably speeds up hierarchical clustering by running on CUDA instead of the CPU. We're talking about 30-150x faster than SciPy depending on the setting.</p> <p>Let's load the pooling-aware model and retrieve with compressed document embeddings. Kernel settings aren't saved with the model, so add use_kernels=True when loading if you'd like to use them for inference too:</p> <p>The pooler compresses the document embeddings after the encoder's forward pipeline, reducing the total from 58 vectors to 16 while leaving query embeddings unchanged. Mars still receives the highest similarity score, followed by Jupiter and Venus, so the ranking is preserved despite storing far fewer document vectors.</p> <p>You can change pool_factor at inference to explore a different storage budget with the same trained model. For repeated use, you can also pass token_pooling=pooling when initializing MultiVectorEncoder to make it the runtime default. The pooler's tasks still control which inputs are compressed (e.g. only documents).</p> <p>To investigate, I trained two models from answerdotai/ModernBERT-base, each with a fresh 128-dimensional token projection:</p> <p>Both runs use one epoch over the same 120,000 MS MARCO triplets, seed 42, and matching initialization and optimization settings. The training token cap is 300, and short queries are expanded to at least 32 token positions to provide additional contextual query vectors. Only the loss differs between the two experiments, and I didn't run a hyperparameter search.</p> <p>I evaluated both models on NanoBEIR@13, reporting mean nDCG@10 (%). The figure compares ordinary and pooling-aware training with pool factors of 2, 3, 4, and 6, alongside unpooled retrieval. The table also includes fixed caps and adaptive thresholds, showing how the training benefits transfer to other pooling settings.</p> <p>For adaptive pooling, I calibrated a separate threshold for each encoder and NanoBEIR corpus, using its unpooled document embeddings to match the average vector counts under caps of 64, 32, and 16. Short documents bring those averages below their respective caps.</p> <p>At the trained pool_factor=4, nDCG@10 improves from 49.03 to 51.23, while storing 74.8% fewer document vectors than unpooled retrieval. This increases score retention from 94.6% to 97.8%, where retention is the pooled mean nDCG@10 divided by each model's own unpooled mean. Unpooled retrieval also improves, from 51.84 to 52.39.</p> <p>The gains extend to fixed caps and adaptive pooling, even though training used only the full representation and proportional pooling. At an average of 29.58 vectors per document, adaptive pooling retains 97.3% of the pooling-aware model's unpooled score while storing 84.7% fewer document vectors. The normally trained model retains 93.3% at the same budget.</p> <p>If index size is your main concern, I would reach for these options in this order:</p> <p>If the model's default dimensionality is larger than 128, I would consider Matryoshka truncation and fine-tuning earlier as well. These approaches can be combined, so evaluate the resulting index size and retrieval quality with your search engine and corpus.</p> <p>MultiVectorMatryoshkaLoss trains token embeddings to remain useful after truncation. You can wrap it with MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss to train for both smaller dimensions and fewer document vectors, reusing the encoder's embeddings across the compression settings.</p> <p>Try the complete training example, choose a budget that matters for your application, and compare it with a matched ordinary-loss run. The accompanying evaluation script measures unpooled retrieval, caps of 64, 32, 16, 8, and 4 vectors, and pool factors of 2 through 6, so you can plot the quality and storage tradeoff for your own model.</p> <p>With a few extra lines in the training objective, a smaller document representation becomes something the model actively learns to use. That opens up an exciting amount of room to make multi-vector retrieval more practical!</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://huggingface.co/blog/token-pooling" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9704"> <h2>#9704. BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/6468b319b2321e47d3267049/Emr86qw6NAueYLdIEiTTD.png" alt="BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information.</p> <p>🤗 Model (safetensors)  |  📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4)</p> <p>We will take appropriate actions in response to notice of copyright infringement. If you believe your work has been used or copied in a manner that infringes upon your intellectual property rights, please email data-apps@tether.io identifying and describing both the copyrighted work and alleged infringing content to file a notice of infringement.</p> <p>BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3).</p> <p>Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards.</p> <p>We first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called.</p> <p>Next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4).</p> <p>Learning from rules and environments (RL stages)</p> <p>Finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth.</p> <p>The second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling.</p> <p>Each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use.</p> <p>BotPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5).</p> <p>Table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.</p> <p>Tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model.</p> <p>Table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.</p> <p>BotPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese.</p> <p>Table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.</p> <p>The largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1).</p> <p>BotPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8).</p> <p>BotPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ.</p> <p>Simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70).</p> <p>On complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks.</p> <p>Complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14).</p> <p>BotPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer.</p> <p>Shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each.</p> <p>Fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9):</p> <p>It does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks.</p> <p>BotPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty.</p> <p>BotPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics.</p> <p>[1] Yu, Qiying, et al. "DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (2025): 113222–113244.</p> <p>[2] Zhang, Shaokun, et al. "Nemotron-Research-Tool-N1: Exploring Tool-Using Language Models with Reinforced Reasoning." International Conference on Learning Representations (2026).</p> <p>[3] Qian, Cheng, et al. "ToolRL: Reward is All Tool Learning Needs." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (2025).</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://huggingface.co/blog/qvac/botpsy" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9702"> <h2>#9702. Mobile Manipulator Foundations and System Architecture — Ch.11: Performance Metrics [EN]</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://dev-to-uploads.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/3otvb2z646ytpt1hl2rv.jpg" alt="Mobile Manipulator Foundations and System Architecture — Ch.11: Performance Metrics [EN]" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>STATERA Library · Series 03 · Volume 01 · Chapter 11 · EN Source: https://github.com/Statera-Library/03_Vol_01_Mobile_Manipulator_Foundations_and_System_Architecture/blob/main/Chapter_11_Performance_Metrics/Chapter_11_Performance_Metrics_EN.md</p> <p>Volume 01. Mobile Manipulator Foundations and System Architecture</p> <p>Mobility metrics provide a quantitative foundation for evaluating how effectively a mobile manipulator moves through its operating environment. Unlike conventional autonomous mobile robots, mobile manipulators must maintain navigation performance while carrying robotic arms, end effectors, and variable payloads. Their mobility performance therefore depends on mechanical design, localization accuracy, motion control, environmental conditions, and coordination between the mobile platform and manipulator.</p> <p>Travel speed is a fundamental mobility metric that describes the distance traveled per unit of time. Maximum speed represents the platform\'s physical capability, while nominal operating speed reflects practical movement under normal conditions. Average mission speed includes acceleration, deceleration, obstacle avoidance, and traffic interruptions. Evaluating these values separately helps engineers distinguish theoretical mobility capability from actual operational performance.</p> <p>Acceleration and deceleration characteristics determine how efficiently a mobile manipulator changes velocity during navigation. Rapid acceleration may improve travel efficiency but can introduce vibration, wheel slip, and disturbances to the robotic arm. Controlled deceleration is particularly important when transporting fragile objects or approaching manipulation stations. Performance evaluation should consider acceleration limits, braking distance, motion smoothness, and payload stability.</p> <p>Positioning accuracy measures the difference between a robot\'s estimated or commanded position and its actual physical location. Accurate positioning is essential when the manipulator must interact with shelves, machines, workstations, or docking interfaces. Positioning errors may originate from wheel odometry, localization algorithms, sensor calibration, or environmental changes. Evaluation should distinguish localization accuracy from final physical positioning accuracy.</p> <p>Positioning repeatability describes the ability of a mobile platform to return consistently to the same target location across repeated trials. A robot may exhibit systematic positioning error while maintaining excellent repeatability, allowing calibration or local correction strategies to compensate. Conversely, inconsistent positioning creates difficulties for robotic manipulation. Repeatability is commonly evaluated through repeated docking experiments and statistical analysis of position deviations.</p> <p>Orientation accuracy is another critical mobility metric because small angular errors can significantly affect the manipulator\'s reachable workspace. When a mobile robot approaches a workstation, incorrect heading may shift the effective position of its end effector. Orientation performance can be measured using angular error, heading repeatability, and rotational stability. These measurements are especially important for narrow workspaces and precision assembly operations.</p> <p>Path tracking accuracy evaluates how closely a mobile manipulator follows a planned trajectory. Common measurements include lateral deviation, heading error, maximum tracking error, and root mean square trajectory error. Tracking performance depends on vehicle kinematics, controller parameters, localization quality, and environmental disturbances. Reliable path tracking reduces unnecessary corrections and supports predictable movement through industrial facilities.</p> <p>Navigation success rate measures the proportion of navigation missions completed according to predefined acceptance criteria. A successful mission typically requires reaching the intended destination without collisions, unsafe behavior, or unacceptable positioning errors. Navigation failures may result from localization loss, inaccessible routes, dynamic obstacles, or controller limitations. Success rates should be evaluated across representative routes, operating conditions, and mission durations.</p> <p>Obstacle avoidance performance measures the robot\'s ability to detect, interpret, and safely navigate around objects within its operating environment. Relevant measurements include detection-to-response latency, minimum obstacle clearance, avoidance success rate, and additional travel distance. Static obstacles provide controlled evaluation conditions, while moving pedestrians and vehicles introduce uncertainty. Testing should account for different obstacle sizes, movement patterns, and sensor visibility.</p> <p>Navigation efficiency describes how effectively the robot reaches its destination relative to an appropriate reference route. Path efficiency can be expressed as the ratio between reference path length and actual traveled distance, provided the reference is feasible and comparable. Excessive detours increase energy consumption and mission duration. However, the shortest path is not necessarily optimal when safety constraints, congestion, or manipulation requirements influence route selection.</p> <p>Turning radius and maneuverability determine whether a mobile manipulator can operate within constrained industrial spaces. Differential-drive platforms can rotate approximately around their own centers, while steering-based platforms may require larger turning areas. Omnidirectional configurations offer additional movement flexibility but introduce mechanical and control complexity. Maneuverability evaluation should include corridor width, turning clearance, lateral motion capability, and obstacle proximity.</p> <p>Terrain traversal capability measures how effectively the mobile platform operates across different surface conditions. Relevant factors include maximum negotiable slope, floor discontinuities, obstacle crossing height, surface friction, and wheel traction. Uneven terrain may affect localization, payload stability, and manipulator calibration. Testing should represent the actual deployment environment rather than relying exclusively on ideal laboratory floors.</p> <p>Payload-dependent mobility performance is especially important because a mobile manipulator\'s mass distribution changes during operation. Payload weight, arm extension, and object placement influence the center of gravity, traction, braking behavior, and tipping resistance. A robot carrying a heavy object with an extended arm may require reduced acceleration or turning speed. Mobility tests should therefore cover representative payload configurations and manipulator postures.</p> <p>Motion stability evaluates unwanted vibration, oscillation, and body movement during travel. Excessive platform vibration can reduce sensor measurement quality, disturb transported objects, and increase mechanical wear. Stability measurements may include linear acceleration, angular velocity, vibration amplitude, and settling time. These metrics become particularly important when mobile manipulators transport delicate components or perform precision operations immediately after navigation.</p> <p>Docking accuracy measures the ability of a mobile manipulator to approach and align with a designated workstation or interface. Successful docking may require precise longitudinal, lateral, and angular positioning. Mechanical guides, visual markers, laser localization, and local correction algorithms can improve alignment. Evaluation should include docking success rate, final pose error, docking duration, and the number of corrective movements required.</p> <p>Localization robustness describes the ability to maintain reliable position estimation under changing environmental conditions. Industrial facilities may contain reflective surfaces, repetitive structures, temporary obstacles, and areas with limited visual features. These conditions can degrade LiDAR, camera, or odometry-based localization. Robustness testing should examine localization failures, recovery time, pose estimation uncertainty, and performance during environmental changes.</p> <p>Recovery performance evaluates how effectively a mobile manipulator resumes navigation after encountering unexpected conditions. Recovery scenarios may include blocked routes, temporary localization failures, emergency stops, or communication interruptions. Useful measurements include recovery success rate, average recovery duration, and the frequency of human intervention. Effective recovery mechanisms improve operational continuity without compromising safety or introducing unpredictable movements.</p> <p>Energy efficiency during mobility describes the electrical energy required to move the robot through representative operating conditions. Energy consumption depends on travel distance, velocity, acceleration, payload mass, terrain, and drive system efficiency. Measurements such as watt-hours per kilometer support comparisons between mobility configurations. For mobile manipulators, propulsion energy should be distinguished from manipulator, perception, computing, and auxiliary power consumption.</p> <p>Mission travel time measures the elapsed duration between departure and arrival at a designated destination. Unlike nominal speed, this metric captures practical delays caused by route planning, obstacle avoidance, congestion, and positioning adjustments. Travel time distributions reveal operational variability that average values may conceal. Percentile-based measurements are useful when evaluating whether a robot can satisfy predictable production schedules.</p> <p>Mobility availability describes the proportion of required operating time during which the navigation subsystem remains capable of performing assigned movements. Mobility interruptions may arise from drive faults, sensor failures, localization problems, or control system errors. Availability measurements should distinguish planned maintenance from unexpected failures. This distinction helps engineers identify whether performance limitations originate from mechanical reliability, software robustness, or operational procedures.</p> <p>Mobility benchmarking requires standardized test conditions to ensure meaningful comparisons between platforms. Test protocols should specify payload mass, floor characteristics, route geometry, obstacle arrangements, velocity limits, and environmental conditions. Each experiment should include sufficient repetitions to estimate variability. Reporting average performance together with dispersion, worst-case observations, and failure frequency provides a more complete understanding of mobility capability.</p> <p>Real-world mobility evaluation should combine controlled laboratory measurements with representative operational trials. Laboratory testing supports repeatable characterization of positioning, tracking, acceleration, and docking behavior. Field testing exposes interactions with pedestrians, equipment, traffic congestion, and changing layouts. Comparing these results reveals the difference between nominal technical performance and the capabilities achievable during sustained deployment.</p> <p>Mobility metrics must ultimately be interpreted within the complete mobile manipulation workflow. High travel speed offers limited value if inaccurate docking increases arm alignment time or causes grasp failures. Similarly, excellent positioning accuracy may not justify excessive navigation delays. Effective system evaluation connects mobility measurements with manipulation readiness, mission completion, safety constraints, and overall task performance to support balanced engineering decisions.</p> <p>Manipulation metrics provide a quantitative framework for evaluating how effectively a mobile manipulator performs physical interactions with objects and its surrounding environment. Unlike fixed industrial robots, mobile manipulators operate from platforms whose positioning accuracy and stability may vary between tasks. Manipulation performance therefore depends on robotic arm precision, perception quality, grasp stability, motion planning, force control, and coordination with the mobile base.</p> <p>Manipulation accuracy measures the difference between the commanded end-effector position and its actual position during task execution. This metric is essential for applications involving assembly, machine tending, object placement, and precision handling. Position errors may originate from joint calibration, mechanical deformation, sensor uncertainty, or mobile platform misalignment. Accuracy should be evaluated under representative payloads, arm configurations, and operating conditions.</p> <p>Manipulation repeatability describes the ability of a robotic arm to return consistently to the same target pose across repeated operations. A manipulator may exhibit systematic positioning errors while maintaining excellent repeatability, allowing calibration procedures to improve absolute accuracy. Repeatability is particularly important in repetitive industrial processes where consistent object placement is required. Evaluation typically involves repeated movements and statistical analysis of positional deviations.</p> <p>End-effector orientation accuracy measures how closely the actual tool orientation matches the commanded orientation. Angular errors can significantly affect insertion, assembly, gripping, and surface interaction tasks. Orientation performance depends on joint encoder resolution, kinematic calibration, mechanical backlash, and controller precision. Evaluation should consider angular deviations around relevant rotational axes and their influence on successful task execution.</p> <p>Grasp success rate represents the proportion of attempted grasps that satisfy predefined success criteria. A successful grasp may require secure object acquisition, stable lifting, transport, and controlled release without unintended slipping or damage. Grasp performance depends on object geometry, surface friction, perception accuracy, and gripper design. Testing should include representative objects, orientations, environmental conditions, and repeated trials.</p> <p>Grasp stability measures the ability of an end effector to maintain secure contact with an object during movement and external disturbances. Stability depends on contact geometry, friction, applied forces, and the object\'s center of mass. Unstable grasps may cause slipping, rotation, or accidental release. Evaluation can incorporate slip frequency, object displacement, contact force variation, and resistance to controlled disturbances during manipulation.</p> <p>Payload capacity describes the maximum object mass that a manipulator can safely handle under specified operating conditions. However, nominal payload ratings do not fully represent performance across the entire workspace. Arm extension, joint torque limits, acceleration, and mobile platform stability influence practical handling capability. Payload evaluation should consider object mass, center-of-mass offset, tool weight, dynamic loading, and allowable motion profiles.</p> <p>Reachability measures the manipulator\'s ability to position its end effector at required locations within the operating environment. The reachable workspace is determined by arm geometry, joint limits, collision constraints, and mobile base placement. Not every reachable position supports every tool orientation or payload. Reachability evaluation should distinguish geometric reach from task-feasible reach and consider whether required manipulation poses can be achieved reliably.</p> <p>Dexterity describes the manipulator\'s ability to perform controlled movements across different positions and orientations. High dexterity enables flexible object handling, complex assembly, and operation within constrained spaces. Dexterity can be analyzed using kinematic manipulability, joint configuration flexibility, and proximity to singularities. These measurements help identify regions where precise motion or force generation becomes difficult despite geometric reachability.</p> <p>Manipulation cycle time measures the elapsed duration required to complete a defined manipulation operation. A typical cycle may include object detection, grasp planning, arm positioning, gripping, lifting, transfer, placement, and release. Cycle time varies with object complexity, motion distance, payload, and controller performance. Separating planning time from physical execution time helps identify whether computational delays or mechanical limitations dominate task performance.</p> <p>Trajectory tracking accuracy evaluates how closely the manipulator follows a planned motion path during execution. Common measurements include Cartesian position error, orientation error, joint tracking error, and maximum trajectory deviation. Tracking performance is influenced by controller bandwidth, actuator dynamics, payload inertia, and mechanical flexibility. Accurate trajectory tracking is especially important for insertion, dispensing, welding, and collision-sensitive operations.</p> <p>Force control accuracy measures the difference between commanded interaction forces and actual forces applied to objects or surfaces. This metric is essential for contact-rich tasks such as polishing, assembly, insertion, and delicate object handling. Force errors may result from sensor calibration, actuator friction, control latency, or structural compliance. Evaluation should consider steady-state force error, transient response, overshoot, and force stability during contact.</p> <p>Impedance and compliance performance describe how a manipulator responds to external forces and environmental constraints. Appropriate compliance allows controlled physical interaction while reducing excessive contact forces. Performance can be evaluated through effective stiffness, damping behavior, displacement under applied loads, and response to disturbances. These characteristics are particularly important when manipulating uncertain objects or interacting with equipment that has limited positioning tolerance.</p> <p>Manipulation planning success rate measures the proportion of task requests for which the planning system produces valid, executable motions. Planning failures may arise from unreachable targets, joint limits, singularities, collisions, or computational constraints. A valid planned trajectory does not necessarily guarantee successful physical execution. Therefore, planning success should be measured separately from execution success, with both evaluated across representative task scenarios.</p> <p>Collision avoidance performance evaluates the manipulator\'s ability to execute movements without unintended contact with surrounding objects, equipment, or the mobile platform. Relevant metrics include minimum clearance, collision frequency, trajectory feasibility, and planning latency. Collision checking should account for the entire arm, attached tools, and transported objects. Dynamic environments introduce additional challenges because obstacles may move during execution.</p> <p>Object placement accuracy measures the difference between the intended object pose and its final pose after release. Placement performance depends on grasp quality, end-effector calibration, object geometry, release dynamics, and environmental contact. Even accurate arm positioning may produce poor placement when objects shift during release. Evaluation should measure translational and rotational placement errors, repeatability, and successful completion within specified tolerances.</p> <p>Manipulation robustness describes the ability to maintain acceptable performance despite variations in objects, environmental conditions, and system parameters. Changes in lighting, object orientation, surface friction, payload distribution, or mobile platform positioning can influence task outcomes. Robustness testing should systematically introduce controlled variations and measure their effects on success rates, execution time, and recovery requirements.</p> <p>Recovery performance evaluates the manipulator\'s ability to respond to unsuccessful grasps, unexpected contact, object displacement, or motion execution failures. Effective recovery may involve releasing an unstable grasp, repositioning the tool, updating perception, or generating a new motion plan. Relevant metrics include recovery success rate, recovery duration, repeated failure frequency, and human intervention requirements. Recovery behavior must remain within defined safety constraints.</p> <p>Manipulation energy consumption measures the electrical energy required to execute physical tasks. Energy demand depends on actuator efficiency, payload mass, joint motion, acceleration, holding torque, and task duration. Measurements such as watt-hours per completed manipulation cycle support comparisons between control strategies and hardware configurations. Energy analysis should distinguish arm actuation from gripper operation, perception processing, and mobile platform consumption.</p> <p>Task completion rate measures the proportion of manipulation tasks successfully completed according to application-specific acceptance criteria. Unlike grasp success rate, this metric evaluates the complete operation, including acquisition, movement, placement, and any required verification. A grasp may succeed while the overall task fails because of incorrect placement or incomplete interaction. Task completion rate therefore provides a broader measure of functional manipulation capability.</p> <p>Mobile base and arm coordination accuracy evaluates how effectively the two subsystems maintain consistent spatial relationships during manipulation. Errors in base localization, coordinate transformations, or platform stabilization can propagate into end-effector positioning errors. Coordinated motion may improve workspace coverage but introduces additional control complexity. Evaluation should consider relative pose accuracy, synchronization delays, and manipulation performance during base movement.</p> <p>Manipulation benchmarking requires standardized objects, task definitions, operating conditions, and acceptance criteria. Test procedures should specify payloads, object geometries, target poses, environmental constraints, and permitted recovery actions. Repeated trials are necessary to estimate performance variability and identify systematic failure patterns. Reporting success rates alongside accuracy, cycle time, and failure distributions supports meaningful comparisons between robotic systems.</p> <p>Manipulation metrics must ultimately be interpreted within the complete mobile manipulation workflow. Excellent arm accuracy provides limited operational value if unreliable navigation prevents access to workstations or unstable grasps cause repeated failures. Similarly, rapid manipulation may be undesirable when it increases object damage or safety risks. Effective evaluation combines precision, reliability, speed, robustness, and physical interaction quality to support balanced system-level optimization.</p> <p>System-level metrics provide an integrated framework for evaluating the overall performance of a mobile manipulator as a coordinated robotic system. Unlike individual mobility or manipulation measurements, these metrics examine how navigation, perception, planning, control, communication, and physical interaction contribute to mission execution. A system may contain high-performance components yet deliver poor results when subsystem integration introduces delays, errors, or operational conflicts.</p> <p>End-to-end task success rate measures the proportion of complete missions that satisfy predefined acceptance criteria. A typical mission may involve navigating to a workstation, identifying an object, grasping it, transporting it, and placing it at a destination. Failure at any critical stage can prevent successful completion. This metric captures the combined effectiveness of mobility, manipulation, perception, and task coordination rather than evaluating each capability independently.</p> <p>Mission completion time represents the total elapsed duration required to execute an assigned workflow. It includes navigation, localization, object recognition, manipulation planning, physical execution, verification, and recovery operations. Measuring only arm movement or travel time can underestimate actual system delays. Decomposing mission duration into functional stages helps engineers identify bottlenecks and prioritize improvements that produce meaningful operational benefits.</p> <p>System throughput measures the number of successfully completed tasks within a specified operating period. Throughput depends on navigation efficiency, manipulation cycle time, task scheduling, resource availability, and environmental conditions. Increasing the speed of one subsystem may not improve throughput if another subsystem remains the limiting factor. System-level throughput analysis therefore emphasizes coordinated optimization rather than isolated component acceleration.</p> <p>System availability describes the proportion of scheduled operating time during which the complete mobile manipulator remains capable of performing assigned tasks. Availability can be reduced by mechanical failures, software faults, sensor problems, communication interruptions, or required maintenance. A functioning mobile base does not guarantee system availability when the robotic arm or perception subsystem is unavailable. Evaluation must therefore consider the operational readiness of all mission-critical components.</p> <p>System reliability measures the probability that a mobile manipulator performs its intended functions without failure during a defined period or mission. Reliability depends on hardware durability, software stability, sensor performance, and integration quality. Repeated minor failures may significantly reduce operational effectiveness even when individual components appear reliable. Mission reliability should be evaluated using representative workloads, environmental conditions, and sufficiently long observation periods.</p> <p>System latency measures the delay between an event, command, or sensor observation and the corresponding system response. Latency may originate from perception processing, network communication, task planning, motion control, or actuator execution. Excessive delays can reduce productivity and compromise coordinated behavior. Evaluation should distinguish average latency from worst-case response times, particularly when timing constraints influence safety or physical interaction.</p> <p>Synchronization accuracy evaluates how consistently distributed subsystems coordinate their operations in time. Mobile manipulators frequently combine sensors, navigation controllers, robotic arms, and edge computing devices operating at different update rates. Timing inconsistencies can produce outdated coordinate transformations or delayed control commands. Synchronization performance can be characterized through timestamp alignment, communication jitter, and coordinated motion errors.</p> <p>System positioning accuracy measures the final spatial accuracy achieved by the complete mobile manipulation system. Unlike isolated arm accuracy, this metric incorporates mobile base positioning, localization uncertainty, coordinate transformations, mechanical compliance, and tool calibration. Small errors from multiple subsystems may accumulate at the end effector. Evaluating final task-space accuracy provides a more realistic measure of the system\'s ability to perform precision operations.</p> <p>Operational robustness describes the ability of the integrated system to maintain acceptable performance under changing conditions. Variations in lighting, floor friction, object placement, network quality, and environmental layout can influence multiple subsystems simultaneously. Robustness testing should introduce representative disturbances while measuring mission success, execution time, and recovery behavior. This approach reveals weaknesses that may remain hidden during isolated component testing.</p> <p>Fault tolerance measures the ability of a mobile manipulator to continue operating safely when selected components experience failures or degraded performance. Redundant sensors, alternative communication paths, diagnostic monitoring, and fallback operating modes can improve fault tolerance. However, not every failure permits continued operation. Evaluation should determine whether the system detects faults, transitions to an appropriate state, and preserves essential safety requirements.</p> <p>System recovery performance evaluates how effectively the robot restores normal operation after interruptions or unsuccessful task execution. Recovery may involve relocalization, motion replanning, object reinspection, manipulator repositioning, or controlled task restarting. Relevant measurements include recovery success rate, recovery duration, repeated failure frequency, and human intervention requirements. Recovery mechanisms should avoid unnecessary repetition and prevent unsafe continuation after critical failures.</p> <p>Resource utilization measures how efficiently the integrated system uses computational, electrical, mechanical, and communication resources. CPU and GPU utilization, memory consumption, network bandwidth, and actuator duty cycles can reveal performance constraints. High resource utilization does not necessarily indicate efficient operation if excessive processing introduces delays or thermal limitations. Evaluation should connect resource consumption with completed tasks and operational requirements.</p> <p>Energy efficiency at the system level measures the total electrical energy consumed during complete missions. Unlike mobility-only or manipulation-only measurements, it includes propulsion, robotic arm actuation, perception sensors, computing hardware, communication equipment, and auxiliary systems. Energy per successful task provides a practical comparison between system configurations. Idle consumption, charging losses, and unsuccessful task attempts should also be considered when defining evaluation boundaries.</p> <p>System stability describes the ability of the mobile manipulator to maintain controlled behavior during navigation, manipulation, and transitions between operating modes. Movement of the robotic arm can alter platform loading and introduce dynamic disturbances. Simultaneous base and arm motion increases coordination requirements. Stability evaluation should consider vibration, body motion, control oscillations, payload displacement, and settling time before precision manipulation.</p> <p>Perception-to-action performance measures how effectively sensor information is transformed into appropriate physical behavior. The process may include sensor acquisition, object detection, pose estimation, decision-making, motion planning, and actuator control. Errors or delays at any stage can degrade task execution. End-to-end evaluation should consider perception accuracy, information freshness, decision latency, and the resulting physical task outcome.</p> <p>Communication performance evaluates the reliability and responsiveness of data exchange between system components. Mobile manipulators may depend on internal field buses, Ethernet networks, wireless connections, and external fleet management systems. Packet loss, excessive jitter, or communication interruptions can disrupt coordination. Relevant measurements include message delivery success, bandwidth utilization, communication latency, and recovery behavior following connection loss.</p> <p>Autonomy level describes the extent to which a mobile manipulator can complete assigned missions without direct human control. Autonomy evaluation should consider independent task execution, environmental adaptation, exception handling, and recovery capability. A system that performs routine tasks automatically but frequently requires assistance during unexpected conditions may have limited practical autonomy. Human intervention frequency and intervention duration provide useful operational measurements.</p> <p>Scalability measures how effectively system performance is maintained when task complexity, operating area, or the number of robots increases. Larger deployments introduce communication traffic, scheduling conflicts, shared resource constraints, and additional coordination requirements. Performance may degrade even when individual robots remain technically capable. Scalability testing should examine throughput, latency, resource utilization, and mission success across increasing workloads.</p> <p>System integration quality reflects how consistently mechanical, electrical, computational, and software components operate together. Interface mismatches, inconsistent coordinate frames, incompatible timing assumptions, and incomplete fault handling can undermine otherwise capable subsystems. Integration performance can be evaluated through interface error frequency, system initialization success, configuration consistency, and cross-subsystem fault propagation.</p> <p>Mission consistency measures the variability of system performance across repeated executions of equivalent tasks. Two systems may achieve similar average completion times while exhibiting substantially different operational predictability. High variability can complicate production scheduling and resource allocation. Statistical measurements such as standard deviation, percentile completion time, and repeated mission success provide insight into consistency under representative operating conditions.</p> <p>System-level benchmarking requires standardized mission definitions, environmental conditions, payload configurations, and acceptance criteria. Benchmarks should evaluate complete workflows rather than relying exclusively on isolated navigation or manipulation tests. Repeated trials help quantify performance variability and identify interactions between subsystems. Results should report success rates, completion times, resource consumption, recovery events, and relevant safety constraints.</p> <p>Effective system-level performance evaluation requires balancing competing engineering objectives. Higher speed may increase energy consumption, aggressive motion may reduce stability, and additional sensing may improve robustness while increasing computational latency. No single metric can fully describe mobile manipulator capability. A comprehensive evaluation framework connects mission success, reliability, timing, precision, autonomy, and resource efficiency to support practical system optimization.</p> <p>Productivity metrics measure how effectively a mobile manipulator converts available operating time and system resources into completed work. Unlike mobility or manipulation metrics, productivity evaluation emphasizes practical output within real operational workflows. A robot may demonstrate excellent technical performance but deliver limited productivity when excessive waiting, repeated failures, or inefficient scheduling reduce its contribution to industrial operations.</p> <p>Task throughput represents the number of successfully completed operations within a defined period. Depending on the application, throughput may be expressed as picks per hour, transferred containers per shift, or completed machine-tending cycles per day. Accurate measurement requires consistent task definitions and acceptance criteria. Throughput should reflect successful outputs rather than attempted operations to avoid overstating actual production capability.</p> <p>Cycle time measures the elapsed duration required to complete one standardized work sequence. For a mobile manipulator, the sequence may include navigation, object identification, grasp planning, picking, transportation, placement, and verification. Cycle time analysis identifies which activities dominate operational duration. Separating productive execution from waiting and recovery delays helps engineers determine where process improvements will generate the greatest benefit.</p> <p>Effective working time describes the portion of scheduled operating time spent performing activities that directly contribute to task completion. Travel, manipulation, and necessary verification may qualify as productive activities depending on workflow requirements. Unplanned waiting, unnecessary repositioning, and repeated unsuccessful actions reduce effective working time. Clear activity classification is essential for consistent productivity measurement across different deployments.</p> <p>Utilization rate measures the proportion of available operating time during which a robot is actively engaged in assigned work. High utilization may indicate effective resource allocation, but continuous operation does not necessarily imply high productivity. A robot repeatedly performing unsuccessful tasks may remain highly utilized while producing little useful output. Utilization should therefore be interpreted alongside task success rate, throughput, and cycle efficiency.</p> <p>Idle time measures periods when a mobile manipulator is operationally available but not executing assigned tasks. Idle conditions may result from insufficient work requests, unavailable workstations, traffic restrictions, or coordination delays. Excessive idle time can indicate poor scheduling or mismatched production capacity.
