Most substantive obligations apply from December 11, 2027, while vulnerability reporting obligations begin earlier, on September 11, 2026.</p> <p>The Cyber Resilience Act requires manufacturers to address cybersecurity throughout product design, development, production, and vulnerability handling. Requirements include risk-based security controls, secure default configurations, vulnerability management, and appropriate security updates. Manufacturers must assess whether their products fall within specific regulatory categories and determine applicable conformity assessment procedures.</p> <p>European machinery legislation also addresses cybersecurity where malicious interference can affect machinery safety. Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 includes requirements concerning protection against corruption of safety-related software and data. These provisions complement broader cybersecurity legislation rather than replacing it. Mobile manipulator manufacturers should coordinate cybersecurity assessments with machinery risk assessments and safety validation.</p> <p>The NIS2 Directive, Directive (EU) 2022/2555, establishes cybersecurity risk-management and incident-reporting obligations for covered entities in designated sectors. Its application depends on organizational characteristics, activities, and national implementation. A robot manufacturer or operator may face obligations under NIS2 independently of product-level requirements. Product compliance and organizational cybersecurity governance must therefore be distinguished.</p> <p>IEC 62443 provides a widely recognized framework for industrial automation and control system cybersecurity. Its standards address system security, component requirements, secure development processes, and organizational responsibilities. Mobile manipulators integrated into industrial facilities can benefit from this framework. Security architecture should consider the robot, fleet management infrastructure, industrial networks, and remote service interfaces.</p> <p>IEC 62443 introduces concepts such as security zones, conduits, and security levels to structure protection against defined threats. Zones group assets with comparable security requirements, while conduits control communication between zones. A mobile robot deployment may separate motion controllers, safety controllers, onboard computers, and fleet servers. Security levels should be derived from risk assessment rather than assigned solely by equipment type.</p> <p>Cybersecurity risk assessment begins by identifying assets, interfaces, potential threats, and operational consequences. Critical assets include navigation maps, robot configurations, control commands, software images, credentials, and operational logs. Attack scenarios may involve unauthorized motion commands, altered mission parameters, malicious firmware, or disrupted communication. Assessment should consider both likelihood and consequences for safety and availability.</p> <p>Secure system architecture applies defense in depth across hardware, software, networks, and operational procedures. Network segmentation, authenticated interfaces, least-privilege access, and restricted services reduce exposure to attacks. Safety-critical controllers should not rely on unrestricted access from general-purpose computing environments. Security boundaries must remain effective during maintenance, diagnostics, remote support, and emergency recovery.</p> <p>Identity and access management ensures that only authorized users and systems can perform permitted actions. Role-based access control can distinguish operators, maintenance technicians, administrators, and remote service personnel. Strong authentication and credential lifecycle management reduce unauthorized access risks. Privileged operations such as changing safety parameters or deploying firmware should require controlled authorization and traceable records.</p> <p>Secure communication protects data exchanged between robots, fleet management systems, cloud services, and external equipment. Encryption and mutual authentication can reduce interception and impersonation risks. Protocol selection must consider latency, reliability, computational resources, and industrial interoperability. Security mechanisms should not introduce unacceptable delays into time-sensitive control or interfere with independently validated safety functions.</p> <p>Software integrity is essential because mobile manipulators depend on complex operating systems, middleware, navigation algorithms, and device firmware. Secure boot, signed updates, and integrity verification can prevent unauthorized software execution. Manufacturers should establish trusted software delivery processes and protect signing credentials. Recovery mechanisms must support restoration after failed updates without creating unsafe operating conditions.</p> <p>Vulnerability management requires continuous identification, assessment, remediation, and communication of security weaknesses. Manufacturers should monitor relevant components, maintain vulnerability disclosure channels, and provide updates according to applicable obligations. Software bills of materials can improve visibility into third-party dependencies. Vulnerability handling processes should cover both onboard software and supporting fleet or remote management services.</p> <p>Open-source software is widely used in robotics, including ROS 2, Linux, communication libraries, and perception frameworks. Open-source adoption does not eliminate manufacturer responsibility for cybersecurity. Dependencies may contain vulnerabilities or become unsupported during a robot\'s service life. Manufacturers should maintain component inventories, monitor security advisories, evaluate patches, and establish controlled software maintenance procedures.</p> <p>Remote fleet management introduces risks because centralized systems may issue commands to numerous mobile manipulators. Compromised fleet credentials or servers could affect multiple robots simultaneously. Security controls should limit command authority, isolate tenants where applicable, and maintain audit trails. Robots should retain appropriate local protective behavior when fleet communication is unavailable or potentially compromised.</p> <p>Wireless connectivity expands the attack surface of mobile robotic systems. Wi-Fi, cellular, Bluetooth, and other radio interfaces require secure configuration and appropriate authentication. Network disruptions, spoofing attempts, and unauthorized access points may affect robot operations. Designers should distinguish ordinary communication failures from malicious interference and ensure that either condition leads to controlled operational responses.</p> <p>Data protection regulations may apply when robots collect personal information through cameras, microphones, access logs, or other sensors. The EU General Data Protection Regulation establishes obligations concerning lawful processing, data minimization, security, and individual rights. Applicability depends on the nature and context of the data processing. Manufacturers and operators must clarify their respective responsibilities for personal data.</p> <p>Cybersecurity testing should include threat modeling, vulnerability scanning, configuration review, and penetration testing where appropriate. Testing must reflect realistic deployment architectures and exposed interfaces. Industrial robotic systems require particular care because intrusive tests can disrupt physical equipment. Test plans should establish safe conditions, authorization boundaries, recovery procedures, and acceptance criteria before execution.</p> <p>Incident response planning addresses security events that could affect robot availability, information integrity, or physical safety. Organizations should establish procedures for detection, containment, investigation, recovery, and required notifications. Operational teams must understand when robots should enter a controlled stop or restricted operating mode. Incident records and lessons learned should inform future software updates and security architecture improvements.</p> <p>Cybersecurity compliance requires evidence demonstrating that relevant requirements have been implemented and maintained. Documentation may include threat models, security requirements, architecture descriptions, software inventories, test reports, and vulnerability handling procedures. Manufacturers should maintain traceability between identified threats and implemented controls. Evidence must reflect the actual deployed configuration and supported software versions.</p> <p>International cybersecurity obligations differ across jurisdictions and application sectors. Some markets emphasize product cybersecurity, while others regulate critical infrastructure operators, data protection, or industrial networks. IEC 62443 and related standards can support technical alignment but do not automatically satisfy every legal requirement. Global manufacturers should establish jurisdiction-specific compliance matrices and monitor regulatory developments.</p> <p>A comprehensive cybersecurity strategy integrates secure development, regulatory analysis, operational monitoring, and lifecycle support. For mobile manipulators, cybersecurity must protect both digital assets and the physical processes controlled by robotic systems. Effective governance connects manufacturers, integrators, operators, and service providers through clearly assigned responsibilities. The objective is resilient robotic operation despite evolving threats and changing deployment conditions.</p> <p>Global compliance strategy for mobile manipulators establishes a coordinated approach to meeting safety, electrical, electromagnetic, cybersecurity, and market-access requirements across jurisdictions. These robots combine autonomous mobility with industrial manipulation, creating regulatory obligations that extend beyond individual components. Effective compliance planning must begin during product architecture development rather than after engineering completion.</p> <p>International regulatory frameworks differ in legal authority, product classification, conformity assessment, and documentation requirements. ISO and IEC standards support technical harmonization, but adopting an international standard does not automatically satisfy national legislation. Manufacturers must distinguish mandatory regulations from voluntary technical standards. This distinction determines which requirements establish legal obligations and which provide evidence of conformity.</p> <p>Product classification is the foundation of a global compliance strategy. A mobile manipulator may be classified as industrial machinery, a mobile industrial robot, an automated guided vehicle, or an integrated robotic system, depending on its functions and operating environment. Classification affects applicable standards, certification procedures, and responsible parties. Engineers should document classification assumptions before selecting the compliance pathway.</p> <p>The European Union applies machinery legislation together with other relevant product regulations. Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 becomes applicable on January 20, 2027, replacing Directive 2006/42/EC. Depending on product configuration, EMC, radio equipment, and cybersecurity legislation may also apply. Manufacturers must identify all applicable instruments and determine the appropriate conformity assessment route before placing products on the market.</p> <p>In the United States, industrial robot compliance involves occupational safety requirements, electrical installation rules, and recognized consensus standards. OSHA regulations establish certain employer obligations, while ANSI and RIA standards provide technical guidance for robotic applications. Product certification and installation acceptance may involve additional authorities or contractual requirements. Compliance responsibilities must be allocated between manufacturers, integrators, and facility operators.</p> <p>Asian markets establish distinct certification and regulatory systems. South Korea applies relevant machinery safety, electrical, electromagnetic compatibility, and radio equipment requirements according to product classification. Japan and China maintain their own product safety and market-access frameworks. Manufacturers should not assume that certification obtained in one country is automatically recognized elsewhere, even when technical requirements reference similar international standards.</p> <p>A regulatory applicability matrix provides a practical mechanism for managing international requirements. The matrix links target markets, product classifications, applicable legislation, standards, conformity assessment procedures, and required evidence. Each requirement should have an assigned owner and verification status. This approach helps engineering teams identify regulatory gaps early and prevents inconsistent interpretations across product variants.</p> <p>Standards selection should reflect the complete robotic application rather than individual equipment categories alone. ISO 10218 addresses industrial robot safety, while ISO 3691-4 and ANSI/RIA R15.08 may be relevant to mobile industrial robot applications. ISO 12100 supports risk assessment, and ISO 13849-1 or IEC 62061 supports safety-related controls. Applicability must be evaluated against the actual machine configuration and intended use.</p> <p>A unified risk assessment process can reduce duplication across jurisdictions while preserving local requirements. Engineers should identify hazards associated with navigation, manipulation, charging, maintenance, and human interaction. Risk reduction measures must be documented and validated under representative operating conditions. Regional compliance differences should be recorded as additional requirements rather than silently incorporated into a single undocumented design assumption.</p> <p>Functional safety architecture should be established early because later modifications can require substantial redesign. Emergency stopping, protective stopping, speed supervision, and movement inhibition must achieve the required safety performance. Mobile manipulators also require coordinated responses between the mobile base and robotic arm. Compliance evidence should demonstrate that combined movements and foreseeable faults do not defeat protective functions.</p> <p>Electrical and EMC compliance requires coordinated evaluation of power distribution, motor drives, battery systems, charging equipment, and communication interfaces. IEC 60204-1, IEC 61000 standards, and applicable drive or battery standards may support engineering verification. Regional differences can affect testing, marking, and documentation. Early pre-compliance testing helps identify weaknesses before formal assessment and reduces costly redesign.</p> <p>Cybersecurity regulations increasingly influence robotic product development and lifecycle management. The EU Cyber Resilience Act introduces obligations for products with digital elements, while industrial cybersecurity standards such as IEC 62443 provide supporting engineering methods. Security requirements should address access control, software integrity, vulnerability handling, and remote connectivity. Manufacturers must distinguish product obligations from requirements imposed on operators.</p> <p>Technical documentation should be organized around traceable engineering evidence rather than separate, inconsistent files for each market. Core records include system specifications, risk assessments, safety calculations, electrical drawings, software configurations, and validation reports. Regional documentation packages can reference this common evidence base. Version control is essential because product changes may invalidate previously completed conformity assessments.</p> <p>Conformity assessment planning should identify whether manufacturer self-assessment, third-party testing, or designated certification procedures are required. Requirements depend on product classification and applicable jurisdiction. Testing laboratories may support EMC, electrical safety, radio, or functional safety verification. Manufacturers should confirm the scope of each assessment and avoid treating a component certificate as proof of complete system compliance.</p> <p>Supplier management is an important part of global compliance. Mobile manipulators incorporate batteries, motor drives, sensors, controllers, wireless modules, and robotic arms obtained from different manufacturers. Supplier declarations and test reports can support integration, but they do not remove system-level responsibility. Procurement specifications should define required certifications, documentation, component traceability, and change notification obligations.</p> <p>Product variants require careful configuration management because regional adaptations can alter compliance assumptions. Changes to wireless modules, battery packs, power supplies, safety sensors, or operating speeds may trigger additional verification. A common hardware and software baseline can simplify certification when supported by documented variant controls. Engineering change procedures should identify regulatory consequences before modifications are released.</p> <p>Installation and commissioning create obligations beyond product manufacturing. Site-specific conditions such as floor geometry, pedestrian traffic, environmental interference, and interaction with surrounding machinery can introduce new hazards. System integrators must validate protective measures within the actual deployment environment. Factory acceptance testing and site acceptance testing should provide complementary evidence without being confused with statutory conformity assessment.</p> <p>Operational compliance continues after deployment through inspection, maintenance, software updates, and incident management. Manufacturers and operators should define responsibilities for maintaining safety configurations and applying security patches. Changes to navigation algorithms, manipulator tools, or fleet management behavior require impact assessment. Records of maintenance, validation, and corrective actions support continued compliance throughout the equipment lifecycle.</p> <p>Global compliance governance benefits from clearly assigned responsibilities across engineering, quality assurance, regulatory affairs, suppliers, and system integrators. Decision records should identify applicable requirements, evidence owners, unresolved risks, and approval authorities. Periodic reviews are necessary because legislation and standards evolve. A controlled compliance register can connect regulatory changes to engineering actions and product release decisions.</p> <p>Market surveillance and post-market obligations must be incorporated into the compliance strategy. Authorities may request technical documentation, investigate unsafe equipment, or require corrective measures. Manufacturers should maintain procedures for handling complaints, reported incidents, and discovered vulnerabilities. Traceability between deployed units, hardware revisions, and software versions enables targeted corrective actions without unnecessarily affecting unaffected products.</p> <p>A phased compliance roadmap can align regulatory activities with engineering milestones. Early development establishes product classification and regulatory scope, followed by architecture reviews and preliminary risk assessments. Integration stages focus on verification, pre-compliance testing, and documentation. Final release requires completion of applicable conformity procedures, while post-market processes maintain the compliance baseline.</p> <p>The objective of global compliance strategy is not merely to obtain certificates but to establish repeatable, evidence-based engineering governance. A well-designed mobile manipulator platform can reuse validated safety functions, electrical architectures, cybersecurity controls, and documentation across multiple markets. Regional differences remain explicit and traceable. This approach supports scalable international deployment while maintaining consistent safety and regulatory accountability.</p> <p>Author: Richard Minsoo Go LinkedIn: Richard Minsoo Go</p> <p>DEV Community — A space to discuss and keep up software development and manage your software career</p> <p>Built on Forem — the open source software that powers DEV and other inclusive communities.</p> <p>Made with love and Ruby on Rails. DEV Community © 2016 - 2026.</p> <p>We're a place where coders share, stay up-to-date and grow their careers.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://dev.to/richard_minsoogo/mobile-manipulator-foundations-and-system-architecture-ch12-standards-and-regulations-en-23lf" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9694"> <h2>#9694. 17 apple dessert recipes for fall baking: Embrace the season with apple tarts, cookies, cakes, and more.</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/sites/default/files/2023-10/Sugar-Crusted-Apple-Cobbler_Hero1.jpg" alt="17 apple dessert recipes for fall baking: Embrace the season with apple tarts, cookies, cakes, and more." style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>There’s an apple dessert for everyone. For the purists, there are lattice-topped pies and shingled galettes. For the non-traditionalists, there are caramel-frosted cakes and fritter-inspired loaves. And for apple lovers that hate cinnamon? Well, there are custardy cakes and classic French tarts. Ready to start baking with fall’s best fruit? Read on for our best apple dessert recipes.</p> <p>There’s no shortage of apple in this cake — applesauce keeps things moist while boiled cider adds sharp, tangy fruit flavor. The cake is great on its own, but pair it with light, creamy Whipped Caramel Frosting, and you’ve got an irresistible baked version of a caramel apple (with none of the fears about your teeth).</p> <p>Get the recipe: Whipped Caramel Apple Cake</p> <p>To make this recipe, you'll need: Vermont Boiled Cider</p> <p>You only need one apple (and two people eager for an apple dessert) to make a pair of these adorable galettes. Half the apple is sliced, while the other half is grated, which creates a hidden layer of jam beneath the shingled slices. Flaky fruit tarts don’t get easier (or cuter!) than this.</p> <p>To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice</p> <p>Get the recipe: Apple Cider Snickerdoodles</p> <p>This super-easy one-bowl cake is loaded with chopped apples and walnuts, which give this moist, spiced cake heft and texture. The frosting, akin to a velvety brown sugar fudge, adds a textural counterpoint and an extra dimension of richness.</p> <p>Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting</p> <p>To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" x 13" pan</p> <p>Cinnamon and apple go together like a flannel and a beanie, but this recipe one-ups that perfect pairing with the addition of cinnamon chips. Diced apple and melty pockets of cinnamon-sugar are also studded throughout these autumnal scones, which are then finished off with an extra-crunchy sugar coating.</p> <p>Get the recipe: Fresh Apple Cinnamon Scones</p> <p>To make this recipe, you'll need: Cinnamon Sweet Bits</p> <p>Ribbons of gooey, cinnamon-scented apples are twisted throughout this striking enriched loaf. Beautiful to behold (and easier to make than you’d think), this braided babka would be a welcome addition to any Rosh Hashanah table or fall celebration.</p> <p>To make this recipe, you'll need: Baker’s Special Dry Milk</p> <p>Spoiler alert: The eponymous secret ingredient in this special pie is boiled cider! Made by cooking down apple cider into a concentrate, a few drops deliver big apple flavor. When used in apple pies, it super-charges the fruit’s tart, tangy flavor, delivering a pie with over-the-top apple goodness.</p> <p>Get the recipe: Secret Ingredient Apple Pie</p> <p>To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider</p> <p>If your go-to doughnut order is an apple fritter, this mash-up cake was made for you. The batter is made using the reverse creaming technique, which ensures a velvety crumb and tender texture. In each slice, there’s a filling and topping of cinnamon-dusted apples and a final drizzle of icy-white vanilla glaze. A slice rivals anything you can get at your local doughnut shop.</p> <p>To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant ClearJel</p> <p>This time of year, apples don't need much to make them shine. The paper-thin, crackly top layer of this cobbler highlights the juicy fruit beneath. It doesn’t need a lot of adornment, but a scoop of vanilla ice cream never hurt anything.</p> <p>Get the recipe: Sugar-Crusted Apple Cobbler Cake</p> <p>To make this recipe, you'll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon</p> <p>Is it a bar? A slab pie? Both! This breezy recipe swaps the flaky pastry for a buttery shortbread crust but keeps the warm, gooey apples and classic spices for a sliceable, portable dessert. To finish, there's a crumbly streusel topping inspired by Dutch apple pie.</p> <p>To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice</p> <p>When you want a fruit dessert fast, you can always count on crisps — no rolling, no resting, and most importantly, no special equipment required! This crisp is made with a handful of baking basics, so when you find yourself with a surplus of apples, dessert is barely an hour away.</p> <p>To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" Square Pan</p> <p>Beneath a buttery, apple-pie-spiced streusel lies a generous layer of tender apples, enriched with intensely flavored boiled cider for a filling that tastes like a truly great apple pie — rich, saucy, and fork-tender apples. The sour cream cake that surrounds the apple filling is plush, subtly tangy, and ultra-moist, providing the perfect counterpoint to the fruit filling and crumb topping.</p> <p>To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice</p> <p>If you’re looking to veer from classic apple pie territory, this galette stays true to those roots but adds a few modern twists. It starts with a buttery whole wheat crust enriched with a touch of sour cream. Then, a layer of apple butter (which can be easily made by cooking down applesauce) is spread beneath a layer of artfully arranged apples slices.</p> <p>Get the recipe: Apple Butter Apple Galette</p> <p>To make this recipe, you'll need: Sparkling Sugar</p> <p>There’s just enough batter to hold together a heap of sliced apples in this one-of-a-kind cake. Gently sweetened with brown sugar and scented with almond extract, this minimalist cake is greater than the sum of its parts — a sophisticated, custardy cake that’s deceivingly simple to make.</p> <p>To make this recipe, you'll need: Almond Extract</p> <p>This pull-apart bread is as fun to make as it is to eat. After rolling out the dough into a rectangle, it’s spread with sweetened apple filling. The dough is cut up into several strips, then stacked and squeezed into a loaf pan. It bakes into a loaf comprised of distinct slices of pillowy apple-studded bread that you can easily tear from the loaf.</p> <p>Get the recipe: Cinnamon-Apple Pull-Apart Bread</p> <p>To make this recipe, you'll need: SAF Instant Yeast</p> <p>The French know a thing or two about baking with apples, and perhaps no recipe is as classic — or elegant — as the Tarte Tatin. Comprised of deeply caramelized apples layered over buttery pastry, it’s a dessert that stuns. Here, we've tested endlessly to ensure this sometimes-fussy dessert goes off without a hitch in your home kitchen.</p> <p>Get the recipe: Classic Apple Tarte Tatin</p> <p>To make this recipe, you'll need: King Arthur Round Cake Pan</p> <p>These handheld treats harness all the nostalgia of a steaming hot McDonald’s fried apple pie but are infinitely better, thanks to the triple threat of a homemade flaky pie crust, a fresh apple filling amplified by boiled cider, and a generous coating of cinnamon sugar.</p> <p>To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider and Apple Pie Spice</p> <p>Looking for more fall baking inspiration? Check out our recipe collection of Fall Favorites.</p> <p>Cover photo by Rick Holbrook; food styling by Kaitlin Wayne.</p> <p>Top tips from the Things Bakers Know podcast.</p> <p>Mini pies may be the secret to a stress-free celebration.</p> <p>See our complete collection of Recipes posts.</p> <p>It’s peak baking season — here’s what to make.</p> <p>Facebook TikTok Instagram Threads Pinterest LinkedIn YouTube Reddit Substack</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2026/09/08/apple-dessert-recipes" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9693"> <h2>#9693. llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/63148d3b996c52bf0142cdbe/2PgU1GxpJX_LVORaP2RRy.png" alt="llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.</p> <p>Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.</p> <p>The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:</p> <p>We are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.</p> <p>The project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.</p> <p>To reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.</p> <p>The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.</p> <p>A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found here.</p> <p>We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.</p> <p>The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors. This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts!</p> <p>Hey, can you guide me with a project? I am not connected.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://huggingface.co/blog/ggml-org/llama-cpp-v1" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9692"> <h2>#9692. Am I ready to sleep? I built a 75-second phone check to answer that</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=1200,height=627,fit=cover,gravity=auto,format=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fgow7rbufghuqnpjt3yvj.jpg" alt="Am I ready to sleep? I built a 75-second phone check to answer that" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge Submission</p> <p>This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge</p> <p>Every night I ask the same question: am I ready to sleep, or do I need a bit more time to get there? For me a good night starts with the state of mind I go to bed in. Sleep trackers tell me how I slept after the fact. I wanted a simple check-in before bed, while I could still try a wind-down routine. So I built Nidra to compare an evening pulse-and-HRV reading with my own recent evenings. It's an experiment, not a prediction of how I'll sleep.</p> <p>Nidra is an Android app. You stand your phone up in room light, close your eyes, and for 75–90 seconds the camera reads your pulse and heart rate variability. You get one number, Sleep Readiness, 0 to 100%, and one thing to try tonight. Then you check again and see before and after.</p> <p>In the morning you drag the same scale to say how rested you feel. Over the week, the history puts your evening number next to your mornings, so you can see whether it's worth listening to.</p> <p>No wearable, no account, no server of Nidra's own. A phone you already own, and your eyes closed.</p> <p>Most sleep trackers tell you how you slept once the night is over. Nidra asks a different question: how ready are you for sleep right now, while you can still do something about it?</p> <p>Nidra is an Android app. Put your phone on a stand, close your eyes for 75–90 seconds, and the camera reads your pulse and heart rate variability. You get one number, Sleep Readiness from 0 to 100%, and one thing to try tonight.</p> <p>Built for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge on DEV.</p> <p>Nidra is a wellness estimate, not a medical device. It doesn't diagnose or treat anything, and it shouldn't guide health decisions.</p> <p>Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, com.presagetech:smartspectra 3.4.0 from Maven Central, MIT licence. The README has setup steps: add your own free Presage API key to local.properties and run on a physical Android phone. There is also a simulated mode that runs every screen without a camera or a key, and 14 unit tests for the scoring, all passing on 13-Nov-2026.</p> <p>The whole SDK integration is one file: SdkVitalsSource.kt.</p> <p>All of this came from checks on my own phone (a Samsung Galaxy M35, which isn't on Presage's tested list).</p> <p>Pulse held steady: 79 to 83 bpm across all three, even hand-held. HRV did not: RMSSD swung from 19 to 76 ms within two minutes, and because Calm is 60% of the score, the score swung from 80% to 45% with it. So one reading isn't something to trust on its own. That's why Nidra compares you with your own median of past evenings and asks for a re-check, and why I'd read it as "roughly where am I tonight", not a precise number.</p> <p>The hand-held check still gave a score, but pulse confidence fell from about 98% to 44% and the camera flagged movement. Holding the phone also means watching the screen, so your eyes stay open (13% closed here). The phone-on-a-stand design with start and end tones exists for exactly that reason.</p> <p>Best Thoughtful Real-World Use. A lot of people go to bed wired and only find out once they're lying awake. Nidra is built for that moment: one number, a dark screen by default, tones so your eyes stay closed, a check short enough to actually do every night, and a refusal to score when the camera can't be trusted. Consent comes first, Nidra keeps its data on the phone, and the consent screen says plainly what the Presage SDK may send (details below).</p> <p>Most Creative or Delightful Use. The same number drives three bedtime themes: Moonlight, where the moon fills from crescent to full; Diya, where a lamp flame grows and steadies as you settle; and Plain, for people who only want the number. The check asks you to close your eyes, so tones, not the screen, tell you when to start and stop.</p> <p>Nidra is a wellness estimate, not a medical device. It makes no diagnosis or treatment claims and doesn't guide health decisions. One evening reading can't predict a night's sleep, which is why it's called readiness, why it's treated as an experiment, and why the history puts your mornings next to it.</p> <p>I built Nidra with help from Claude Code. The testing, the decisions about what to drop, and the evenings in front of the camera were mine.</p> <p>DEV Community — A space to discuss and keep up software development and manage your software career</p> <p>Built on Forem — the open source software that powers DEV and other inclusive communities.</p> <p>Made with love and Ruby on Rails. DEV Community © 2016 - 2026.</p> <p>We're a place where coders share, stay up-to-date and grow their careers.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://dev.to/rahulrao85/am-i-ready-to-sleep-i-built-a-75-second-phone-check-to-answer-that-2mbl" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9691"> <h2>#9691. Mobile Manipulator Foundations and System Architecture — Ch.13: Product Strategy [EN]</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://dev-to-uploads.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/3otvb2z646ytpt1hl2rv.jpg" alt="Mobile Manipulator Foundations and System Architecture — Ch.13: Product Strategy [EN]" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>STATERA Library · Series 03 · Volume 01 · Chapter 13 · EN Source: https://github.com/Statera-Library/03_Vol_01_Mobile_Manipulator_Foundations_and_System_Architecture/blob/main/Chapter_13_Product_Strategy/Chapter_13_Product_Strategy_EN.md</p> <p>Volume 01. Mobile Manipulator Foundations and System Architecture</p> <p>Market analysis for mobile manipulators begins with understanding how autonomous mobility and robotic manipulation create new opportunities across industrial and service environments. Unlike conventional industrial robots operating at fixed workstations, mobile manipulators can travel between locations, interact with physical objects, and execute multiple tasks. Their commercial potential depends on measurable productivity improvements, operational flexibility, and the economic value of automation.</p> <p>The mobile manipulator market exists at the intersection of autonomous mobile robots, industrial robotic arms, collaborative robots, and intelligent automation software. Each segment contributes technologies, suppliers, and established customer expectations. However, combining these capabilities introduces additional complexity in navigation, manipulation, safety, and system integration. Market analysis must therefore evaluate the complete solution rather than treating the robot as a collection of independent components.</p> <p>Industrial manufacturing represents an important potential market because production facilities increasingly require flexible automation across multiple workstations. Mobile manipulators can support machine tending, component transportation, inspection, and material handling without requiring permanent robot installations at every location. Their economic attractiveness increases when one robot can perform several tasks while maintaining acceptable cycle times, positioning accuracy, and operational reliability.</p> <p>Warehouse and logistics operations provide another promising application environment. Traditional autonomous mobile robots primarily transport goods, while mobile manipulators can additionally retrieve, place, sort, and transfer individual objects. This combination may reduce manual handling between transportation and processing stages. Market demand depends on order variability, inventory characteristics, picking complexity, throughput requirements, and the availability of alternative automation solutions.</p> <p>Healthcare facilities present opportunities for mobile manipulators capable of transporting medical supplies and interacting with storage equipment. Potential applications include pharmacy logistics, laboratory sample handling, linen distribution, and automated inventory replenishment. However, hospitals impose demanding requirements for hygiene, reliability, human interaction, and operational continuity. Commercial feasibility depends on integrating robotic workflows with existing hospital infrastructure and administrative procedures.</p> <p>Service robotics introduces additional market segments, including hospitality, retail, airports, offices, and public facilities. Mobile manipulators may support inventory handling, object delivery, equipment assistance, and repetitive service activities. These environments are often less structured than industrial facilities and require sophisticated perception and interaction capabilities. Market adoption depends on customer acceptance, operational safety, task reliability, and the practical benefits compared with conventional service methods.</p> <p>Market segmentation should consider industry, application, operating environment, payload requirements, manipulation complexity, and expected autonomy. A manufacturing customer requiring precise machine loading has fundamentally different needs from a hospital seeking automated supply distribution. These differences influence hardware architecture, software functionality, safety design, and pricing. Effective segmentation identifies groups of customers sharing sufficiently similar requirements to support scalable product development.</p> <p>Geographical market analysis must account for differences in labor costs, industrial automation maturity, regulatory frameworks, and investment conditions. Regions with established manufacturing ecosystems may prioritize productivity and equipment integration, while logistics-intensive economies may emphasize flexible material handling. Local infrastructure, technical support availability, and customer procurement practices also influence adoption. Regional opportunities should be assessed using comparable operational and economic criteria.</p> <p>Market sizing provides a quantitative foundation for investment and product planning. Total Addressable Market represents the broad revenue opportunity under defined assumptions, while Serviceable Available Market narrows that opportunity to applications the product can realistically address. Serviceable Obtainable Market estimates the portion potentially captured within a specific planning period. These calculations require transparent assumptions regarding customer populations, deployment quantities, pricing, replacement cycles, and adoption rates.</p> <p>A bottom-up market estimation approach is particularly useful for emerging robotic products because broad automation statistics may not accurately represent mobile manipulation opportunities. Analysts can estimate the number of suitable facilities, identify applicable workflows, calculate potential robot deployments, and determine expected revenue per installation. Sensitivity analysis should examine how changes in adoption rates, robot utilization, system pricing, and deployment constraints affect the estimated market opportunity.</p> <p>Customer demand should be evaluated through operational problems rather than technological enthusiasm alone. Organizations generally invest in robotics to reduce repetitive labor, improve process consistency, increase throughput, address workforce shortages, or enhance workplace safety. A mobile manipulator must demonstrate a credible connection between its capabilities and these objectives. Customer interviews, facility observations, workflow measurements, and pilot projects provide evidence of whether proposed applications solve meaningful operational problems.</p> <p>The competitive landscape includes manufacturers of autonomous mobile robots, industrial manipulators, collaborative robots, integrated robotic systems, and specialized automation equipment. Competition also comes from fixed automation, conveyors, manually operated vehicles, and conventional labor-intensive processes. Market analysis must compare these alternatives according to complete workflow performance. A technically advanced mobile manipulator may still be commercially unattractive if simpler equipment provides equivalent productivity at lower cost.</p> <p>Technology readiness significantly influences the timing of market adoption. Navigation, localization, object recognition, grasp planning, and coordinated motion control must operate reliably under realistic conditions. Demonstrations in controlled environments do not necessarily establish commercial readiness. Market assessments should distinguish experimental capabilities from validated production performance, considering failure recovery, maintenance requirements, environmental variability, and the degree of human supervision needed during routine operations.</p> <p>Economic evaluation should extend beyond the initial purchase price. Total Cost of Ownership includes integration, infrastructure modifications, software licensing, maintenance, energy consumption, operator training, and technical support. Return on Investment depends on measurable benefits such as labor-hour savings, increased equipment utilization, reduced handling errors, and improved operational availability. Financial models should also account for deployment delays, utilization uncertainty, and the cost of manual intervention.</p> <p>Different commercial models may influence customer adoption. Direct equipment sales provide asset ownership but often require substantial initial capital expenditure. Leasing and Robotics as a Service can distribute costs over time and potentially reduce financial barriers. Subscription arrangements may include maintenance, software updates, fleet monitoring, and operational support. Market analysis should evaluate customer preferences for capital expenditure versus operating expenditure alongside the provider\'s financing and service obligations.</p> <p>Adoption barriers frequently arise from integration complexity rather than robot capability alone. Manufacturing facilities may require connections to production execution systems, programmable logic controllers, and industrial equipment. Warehouses may depend on warehouse management systems, while hospitals operate specialized information platforms. Successful deployment requires compatible interfaces, reliable communication, cybersecurity controls, and clear operational responsibilities. These requirements can substantially influence project costs and implementation schedules.</p> <p>Safety and regulatory requirements also shape market accessibility. Mobile manipulators combine moving platforms with articulated mechanisms, creating hazards that differ from those associated with stationary industrial robots or transportation-only mobile robots. Customers must consider collision risks, emergency stopping, human proximity, and environmental constraints. Applicable standards and conformity assessment obligations vary by deployment context and jurisdiction. Compliance readiness can become a competitive advantage when supported by documented verification procedures.</p> <p>Market growth is influenced by broader developments in artificial intelligence, edge computing, sensor technology, battery systems, and robotic software. Improvements in perception and task planning may expand the range of objects and environments that mobile manipulators can handle. Nevertheless, increased computational capability does not automatically produce commercially reliable autonomy. Product planners must distinguish technological potential from capabilities that have been validated under representative operational conditions.</p> <p>Workforce conditions represent another important demand factor. Labor shortages, employee turnover, repetitive work, and ergonomic risks can encourage organizations to investigate robotic automation. However, automation does not eliminate the need for human participation. Operators may remain responsible for exception handling, supervision, maintenance, and process improvement. Market analysis should evaluate how robotic deployment changes workforce responsibilities and whether customers possess the organizational capabilities required to manage these transitions.</p> <p>Early market opportunities are often concentrated in workflows with predictable objects, controlled environments, and measurable performance targets. These characteristics reduce technical uncertainty and simplify economic validation. Applications involving highly variable objects, unstructured environments, or complex human interaction may require additional development before widespread deployment. Prioritizing technically feasible and economically valuable applications allows manufacturers to accumulate operational evidence while progressively expanding product capabilities.</p> <p>Pilot deployment analysis provides an essential bridge between market assumptions and commercial decisions. A pilot should establish baseline performance, define measurable acceptance criteria, and evaluate the robot under representative operating conditions. Important observations include successful task completion, intervention frequency, cycle time, system availability, and integration effort. Results should be compared with the original business case to determine whether broader deployment is justified or additional engineering work is necessary.</p> <p>Market analysis must also consider the scalability of the supplier\'s business model. A product requiring extensive customization for every installation may generate early project revenue but struggle to achieve sustainable growth. Standardized hardware platforms, configurable software modules, reusable integration interfaces, and repeatable deployment procedures can improve scalability. The proportion of engineering effort that can be reused across customers is therefore an important indicator of long-term commercial viability.</p> <p>Distribution channels and partnerships influence market penetration. System integrators, industrial equipment suppliers, software providers, and regional service organizations may help manufacturers reach customers and deliver complete solutions. Partnerships can reduce deployment barriers by combining specialized technical capabilities and established customer relationships. However, channel strategies must clarify responsibility for integration, warranties, maintenance, cybersecurity, and operational performance to prevent fragmented customer support.</p> <p>Competitive differentiation should be based on attributes that customers can verify and value. Potential differentiators include manipulation accuracy, navigation reliability, payload capacity, task flexibility, deployment simplicity, safety performance, and software interoperability. Superior specifications alone may not justify premium pricing. Sustainable differentiation emerges when technical advantages produce measurable operational benefits and are supported by reliable service, documented performance, and continuous product improvement.</p> <p>Long-term market forecasting requires multiple scenarios because emerging robotics markets contain substantial uncertainty. Conservative scenarios may assume slow customer adoption, extensive integration requirements, and limited autonomous task coverage. More optimistic scenarios may reflect improved hardware affordability, standardized interfaces, and advances in robotic intelligence. Scenario planning helps manufacturers align research investment, production capacity, staffing, and financial commitments with plausible commercial outcomes rather than a single growth projection.</p> <p>A comprehensive market analysis ultimately connects customer needs, technological feasibility, competitive alternatives, and financial performance. Its purpose is not merely to estimate how many robots might be sold, but to determine where mobile manipulation creates defensible economic value. By continuously validating market assumptions against customer evidence and operational results, manufacturers can establish realistic product priorities, reduce commercialization risks, and build a foundation for sustainable expansion across industrial and service markets.</p> <p>Customer requirements form the foundation of successful mobile manipulator product development because they connect technological capabilities with practical operational needs. A mobile manipulator must satisfy expectations related to mobility, manipulation, safety, reliability, and economic performance. Understanding these requirements allows manufacturers to avoid unnecessary complexity while developing systems that deliver measurable value within specific industrial and service environments.</p> <p>Requirements engineering begins by identifying stakeholders who influence the purchasing, deployment, operation, and maintenance of robotic systems. These stakeholders may include production managers, warehouse supervisors, safety engineers, maintenance technicians, information technology specialists, and financial decision-makers. Each group evaluates the robot from a different perspective, making systematic stakeholder analysis essential for establishing balanced product requirements.</p> <p>Customer interviews and operational observations provide important information about existing workflows and automation opportunities. Interviews reveal perceived problems, while direct observations expose physical constraints, repetitive activities, and operational exceptions that customers may overlook. Engineers should examine how materials move, how workers interact with equipment, and where delays occur before proposing a mobile manipulation solution.</p> <p>Functional requirements describe the activities a mobile manipulator must perform to satisfy its intended purpose. These activities may include autonomous navigation, object detection, grasping, transportation, placement, inspection, and interaction with industrial equipment. Requirements should define complete workflows rather than isolated capabilities because commercial value depends on successful task execution across multiple interconnected operations.</p> <p>Mobility requirements establish how the robot travels through its operating environment. Important considerations include maximum speed, turning radius, localization accuracy, obstacle avoidance, floor conditions, and navigation reliability. A robot operating in a narrow warehouse aisle requires different mobility characteristics from one serving large manufacturing areas. Environmental measurements should guide the selection of drive mechanisms, sensors, and navigation algorithms.</p> <p>Manipulation requirements define the robot\'s ability to interact with physical objects and equipment. Payload capacity, reach, degrees of freedom, positioning repeatability, grasp stability, and end-effector compatibility are important design parameters. These characteristics must correspond to actual object dimensions, weights, materials, and handling conditions. Excessive specifications can increase system cost without improving customer productivity.</p> <p>Mobility and manipulation must also be evaluated as an integrated system. Arm movement changes the robot\'s center of gravity and may influence stability, particularly when handling heavy objects at extended reach. Customers may require manipulation while stationary or during controlled movement. These operating modes create different requirements for base stabilization, coordinated control, localization accuracy, and collision prevention.</p> <p>Performance requirements translate customer expectations into measurable engineering targets. Typical indicators include task completion rate, cycle time, navigation accuracy, manipulation success rate, system availability, and intervention frequency. Requirements should specify operating conditions and acceptance thresholds so that performance can be verified objectively. Ambiguous expectations such as fast operation or high reliability are insufficient for engineering validation.</p> <p>Operational productivity is frequently more important than maximum theoretical robot speed. A mobile manipulator may navigate quickly but lose productivity through slow grasp planning, repeated localization adjustments, or frequent recovery operations. Customer requirements should therefore emphasize end-to-end workflow efficiency. Measuring completed tasks per hour, successful transfers per shift, and effective utilization provides a more meaningful assessment of operational value.</p> <p>Safety requirements are essential because mobile manipulators operate near people, machinery, and valuable equipment. Customers may require protective sensing, emergency stopping, speed limitation, collision avoidance, and controlled recovery procedures. Safety engineering must consider hazards arising from both the mobile platform and articulated manipulator. Risk assessment should identify foreseeable misuse, environmental hazards, and interactions between automated and manual activities.</p> <p>Environmental requirements determine whether a robot can operate reliably under actual facility conditions. Temperature, humidity, dust, vibration, lighting variation, floor irregularities, and electromagnetic interference may influence system performance. Industrial environments can expose sensors and actuators to contamination or mechanical disturbances. Requirements should identify acceptable environmental ranges and specify protective measures necessary for continuous operation.</p> <p>Power and battery requirements directly affect operational availability. Customers may specify minimum operating duration, charging time, energy consumption, and battery replacement procedures. These expectations must account for simultaneous navigation, manipulation, perception, and computing workloads. Automated charging and mission resumption may be necessary for extended operation. Energy management should support the customer\'s shift patterns rather than rely solely on nominal battery capacity.</p> <p>System integration requirements describe how the robot communicates with existing equipment and software infrastructure. Manufacturing customers may require interfaces to programmable logic controllers, manufacturing execution systems, and production machinery. Warehouse operators may require warehouse management system connectivity. Standardized communication protocols, documented application programming interfaces, and reliable data exchange reduce integration complexity and support future system expansion.</p> <p>Human-robot interaction requirements define how operators supervise, command, and collaborate with mobile manipulators. User interfaces should provide clear mission status, understandable fault messages, and accessible recovery procedures. Operators may need manual control, task reassignment, or emergency intervention capabilities. Effective interaction design reduces training requirements and prevents operational errors while maintaining appropriate separation between routine controls and safety functions.</p> <p>Reliability and maintainability requirements strongly influence long-term customer satisfaction. Customers expect predictable operation, manageable maintenance intervals, and rapid restoration after failures. Requirements may include diagnostic logging, modular component replacement, remote monitoring, and spare-parts availability. Mean Time Between Failures and Mean Time to Repair provide useful reliability indicators when measured under representative operating conditions and supported by sufficient operational data.</p> <p>Cybersecurity requirements become increasingly important as mobile manipulators connect to enterprise networks, cloud services, and fleet management platforms. Customers may require encrypted communication, authentication, access control, secure software updates, and audit logging. Security architecture should protect operational commands and sensitive information without compromising real-time control. Requirements must also address software maintenance, vulnerability management, and responsibilities throughout the product lifecycle.</p> <p>Scalability requirements determine whether a solution can expand from an initial pilot deployment to multiple robots across facilities. Customers may expect centralized mission scheduling, traffic coordination, fleet monitoring, and consistent software configuration. Product architecture should support additional robots without requiring extensive redesign. Scalability evaluation must consider communication bandwidth, infrastructure capacity, task allocation efficiency, and operational management complexity.</p> <p>Economic requirements define the financial boundaries within which a product must operate. Customers may specify acquisition budgets, operating costs, expected payback periods, and acceptable maintenance expenses. These constraints influence hardware selection, software licensing, deployment methods, and service arrangements. A technically capable robot may still fail commercially if integration and operational costs exceed the measurable benefits delivered to the customer.</p> <p>Customer requirements also vary according to industry-specific workflows. Manufacturing facilities may prioritize precision and equipment synchronization, while warehouses emphasize throughput and inventory handling. Hospitals may require hygiene, quiet operation, and dependable interaction with staff. Service environments may place greater importance on appearance, accessibility, and user acceptance. Product teams should distinguish common platform requirements from application-specific adaptations.</p> <p>Requirements prioritization is necessary because customers often request capabilities that conflict with cost, schedule, or technical feasibility. A larger payload may require heavier actuators and batteries, while increased mobility may demand a compact platform. Engineers should evaluate these tradeoffs using operational value, implementation risk, and development cost. Prioritization helps identify essential functions and separates immediate product needs from potential future enhancements.</p> <p>Traceability connects customer expectations to system specifications, engineering decisions, and verification results. Each important requirement should have an identifiable source, measurable acceptance criterion, and corresponding validation method. Traceability allows development teams to evaluate the consequences of design changes and identify unresolved requirements. It also supports communication between customers, system architects, software developers, and safety engineers throughout development.</p> <p>Prototypes and pilot deployments provide opportunities to validate requirements before commercial production. Real-world testing may reveal unexpected obstacles, object variations, workflow dependencies, or operator preferences. Feedback should be translated into documented requirement updates rather than informal design modifications. Iterative validation reduces the risk of delivering a technically successful system that does not adequately support the customer\'s actual operations.</p> <p>Requirement management must continue after deployment because customer workflows and operating conditions can change. New products, facility layouts, production schedules, and regulatory expectations may introduce additional demands. Software updates and modular hardware improvements can address some changes without replacing the entire robot. A structured change-management process helps maintain compatibility, safety, and product consistency while supporting evolving customer needs.</p> <p>Successful customer requirement analysis ultimately transforms operational problems into clear, measurable, and economically justified product specifications. It aligns mobility, manipulation, software, safety, and service capabilities with the conditions under which customers actually operate. By maintaining continuous communication and validating assumptions through practical evidence, manufacturers can develop mobile manipulators that achieve reliable performance, customer acceptance, and sustainable commercial value.</p> <p>Product positioning defines how a mobile manipulator is perceived by target customers relative to competing robotic solutions and conventional automation methods. It establishes the product\'s intended market role, primary value proposition, and distinguishing characteristics. Effective positioning connects technical capabilities with operational benefits, allowing customers to understand why a particular mobile manipulator is appropriate for their applications and investment priorities.</p> <p>The positioning process begins with identifying the target customer segment and its most important operational challenges. Manufacturing companies may prioritize equipment utilization and flexible production, while warehouses emphasize throughput and material handling efficiency. Hospitals and service organizations may value reliability, safety, and ease of interaction. A product designed to satisfy every market simultaneously may lack the specialization required to achieve meaningful competitive differentiation.</p> <p>A value proposition explains the measurable benefits customers receive from adopting a mobile manipulator. These benefits may include reduced manual handling, increased equipment utilization, improved workflow flexibility, and more consistent task execution. Strong positioning communicates outcomes rather than merely listing technical specifications. Customers should understand how autonomous navigation and robotic manipulation combine to solve problems that conventional mobile robots or fixed manipulators cannot address efficiently.</p> <p>Mobile manipulators occupy a distinctive position between autonomous mobile robots and stationary industrial robotic systems. Autonomous mobile robots primarily transport materials, while fixed manipulators perform localized physical operations. Mobile manipulators integrate both capabilities to execute distributed manipulation tasks across multiple locations. Their positioning should emphasize this integration while acknowledging additional system complexity, safety considerations, and operational limitations.</p> <p>Performance-based positioning focuses on measurable characteristics such as payload capacity, manipulation accuracy, navigation reliability, task completion rate, and operational availability. These attributes are especially important in industrial environments where productivity and process consistency determine purchasing decisions. Performance claims should be supported by standardized testing and representative deployment results rather than isolated demonstrations under favorable conditions.</p> <p>Cost-oriented positioning targets customers seeking economically accessible automation solutions. A competitively priced mobile manipulator may prioritize standardized components, simplified integration, and essential task capabilities over advanced optional functions. However, low acquisition cost does not necessarily produce low total ownership cost. Effective positioning must consider installation expenses, maintenance requirements, software licensing, energy consumption, and expected operational lifetime.</p> <p>Premium positioning emphasizes advanced capabilities, high reliability, extensive integration options, and comprehensive technical support. Such products may incorporate sophisticated perception systems, precision manipulators, redundant sensing, and advanced task planning. Customers may accept higher prices when these capabilities address demanding applications or reduce operational risks. Premium positioning requires demonstrable benefits that justify additional investment throughout the product lifecycle.</p> <p>Application-specific positioning can provide stronger differentiation than general-purpose capability claims. A mobile manipulator optimized for CNC machine tending may emphasize precise docking, equipment communication, and repeatable part handling. A warehouse picking robot may prioritize object recognition, grasp success, and order fulfillment throughput. Specialization allows manufacturers to align hardware, software, and service capabilities with clearly defined customer workflows.</p> <p>Platform positioning emphasizes modularity and adaptability across multiple applications. A common mobile base may support different robotic arms, end effectors, sensor configurations, and software modules. This approach can reduce development duplication and simplify maintenance while supporting a broader product portfolio. Nevertheless, excessive configurability may increase integration complexity, making standardized interfaces and validated configurations essential for scalable deployment.</p> <p>Safety-oriented positioning is particularly relevant when robots operate near human workers or within sensitive environments. Customers may value protective sensing, controlled motion, emergency stopping, and documented risk assessment procedures. Safety should not be presented merely as an optional premium feature because fundamental protection is necessary for responsible deployment. Differentiation may instead arise from verified safety performance, transparent documentation, and simplified compliance processes.</p> <p>Reliability-based positioning emphasizes predictable operation and reduced operational disruption. Industrial customers often prioritize system availability, recovery capability, and maintenance efficiency over experimental autonomy features. Products with comprehensive diagnostics, modular replacement procedures, and dependable technical support may provide greater practical value than systems offering impressive demonstrations but uncertain production performance. Reliability claims require sustained operational evidence.</p> <p>Software capabilities increasingly influence product positioning because mobile manipulators depend on perception, navigation, manipulation planning, and fleet coordination. Products may differentiate through intuitive task configuration, interoperability, remote monitoring, and software update mechanisms. Advanced artificial intelligence can expand task flexibility, but commercial positioning should distinguish validated autonomous capabilities from experimental functions that still require extensive supervision.</p> <p>Integration simplicity can become a major competitive advantage in facilities with existing automation infrastructure. Customers may prefer robots that communicate with manufacturing execution systems, warehouse management platforms, and industrial controllers through documented interfaces. Reduced deployment time and predictable integration effort can improve investment returns. Positioning should therefore emphasize complete system compatibility rather than isolated hardware performance.</p> <p>Customer experience also contributes to market differentiation. Clear user interfaces, understandable diagnostic messages, straightforward operator training, and responsive technical support can improve adoption. In environments where employees interact frequently with robots, usability influences both productivity and acceptance. Manufacturers should evaluate the complete customer journey, including purchasing, installation, commissioning, operation, maintenance, and future upgrades.</p> <p>Brand positioning communicates the manufacturer\'s identity and long-term commitment to the market. A robotics company may emphasize engineering reliability, industrial expertise, artificial intelligence innovation, or customer-focused service. These claims should remain consistent with demonstrated capabilities and organizational resources. Credible branding depends on alignment between marketing communication, product performance, technical documentation, and customer experience.</p> <p>Competitive positioning requires systematic comparison with alternative solutions. Relevant competitors include mobile robot manufacturers, collaborative robot suppliers, integrated automation providers, and conventional equipment vendors. Comparisons should consider complete workflows, deployment requirements, operating costs, and achievable productivity. A positioning strategy becomes more credible when it identifies specific advantages and limitations rather than claiming universal superiority.</p> <p>Pricing strategy must reinforce the intended market position. Entry-level products may use standardized configurations and transparent pricing to reduce purchasing complexity. Higher-end systems may justify premium prices through advanced functionality, specialized engineering, and comprehensive support. Subscription services and Robotics as a Service arrangements can further influence positioning by shifting customer attention from equipment ownership toward delivered operational outcomes.</p> <p>Market positioning should also reflect the customer\'s technology adoption readiness. Early adopters may accept greater technical uncertainty in exchange for innovative capabilities and strategic advantages. Mainstream industrial customers typically require proven reliability, predictable integration, and established service arrangements. Manufacturers must align product maturity, validation evidence, and commercial commitments with the expectations of their intended customer segment.</p> <p>Regional differences can influence positioning because labor economics, industrial practices, infrastructure, and regulatory requirements vary across markets. A product positioned around labor efficiency in one region may be marketed primarily for operational flexibility or quality consistency elsewhere. Localization may require changes in interfaces, documentation, certification, and service delivery. The core value proposition should remain coherent while accommodating legitimate regional requirements.</p> <p>Positioning decisions directly influence product architecture and development priorities. A system marketed for precision industrial manipulation requires appropriate mechanical rigidity, localization accuracy, and calibration procedures. A product emphasizing rapid deployment may prioritize modular hardware and simplified software configuration. When positioning and engineering decisions are inconsistent, manufacturers risk creating products that fail to satisfy their advertised value proposition.</p> <p>Product positioning should be validated through customer interviews, competitive evaluations, and pilot deployments. Customers can assess whether proposed benefits correspond to meaningful operational improvements and whether the product differs sufficiently from available alternatives. Feedback may reveal that initially emphasized features are less valuable than reliability, service quality, or integration simplicity. Evidence-based refinement helps prevent positioning strategies from becoming disconnected from market realities.</p> <p>Positioning must evolve as technology and customer expectations change. Improvements in robotic perception, manipulation intelligence, computing hardware, and system integration may alter competitive boundaries.
