When Scientists Admit Mistakes, That Means Science Is Working</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://ggsc.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/assets/images/anthony_fauci_-_abcdef_-_0a21b39134b316e51cdc0dd96c5e6bca3c0093e9-fb_-_abcdef_-_94b15742ccdfc3b16fb1fe35872167fe8d42c35d.webp" alt="When Scientists Admit Mistakes, That Means Science Is Working" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.</p> <p>Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education</p> <p>When the first cases of COVID-19 were discovered in a hospital in Wuhan, I had already studied the U.S. public health response to seven epidemics and pandemics. I am no stranger to the role of politics in pandemic response. Still, the recent Senate hearings grilling Dr. Anthony Fauci alarmed me.</p> <p>Fauci is a physician and immunologist who served as the director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases and as chief medical advisor to President Trump during the period of Covid-19—who has subsequently become a scapegoat for those who didn’t like the restrictions that came with the pandemic. As Senator Rand Paul put it, based on the evidence-free conspiracy theory that Dr. Fauci funded research that led to the pandemic: “One million Americans died from COVID and not even an apology from Dr. Anthony Fauci.”</p> <p>While we might recognize such claims as preposterous, it would be a mistake to treat these hearings as mere political theater. Those who are treating errors in the understanding of Covid-19 as criminal threaten one of the most important public goods we have during an infectious disease crisis: the willingness of experts to publicly admit mistakes.</p> <p>Dr. Fauci has openly acknowledged missteps, communication errors, and evolving judgments in responding to the COVID-19 pandemic—an honesty that is not matched by his critics. Instead, his honesty has been leveraged by them to sow doubt in science itself.</p> <p>But the reason we turn to experts during a crisis is not because they are omniscient. Of course they aren’t. It is because they learn faster and better than non-experts. Learning, however, is a naturally error-prone process. And learning when a novel infectious disease is fueling a global pandemic is particularly so. One can hope that scientists responding to such a crisis will be able to reduce uncertainties in a linear and predictable fashion. But that is not the norm.</p> <p>As a social scientist, if I discover something new, when I present my findings to my colleagues, the most likely result is that they will tell me all the ways they think I might be wrong. My job is to prove that my findings hold even after considering their counterarguments. Skepticism is essential in the process of separating fact from fiction. We have more confidence in results that have survived such pressure-testing.</p> <p>Experts at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) during the pandemic received just this type of skepticism from other experts. And yet much of the political commentary surrounding these normal and essential controversies cited the evidence of controversy as proof the CDC was flailing.</p> <p>This approach treats science as though the discovery of new facts unfolds like a treasure hunt where the first person to find the treasure opens the lid and everyone can see the treasure with their own eyes. In a treasure hunt, discovery and validation are essentially the same thing.</p> <p>But science does not work this way. Take the discovery of HIV. Dr. Luc Montaignier identified the virus under an electron microscope in February 1983. Uncertainty surrounding whether the virus was causative or opportunistic led to more than a year of additional research, culminating in four papers published by Dr. Robert Gallo and his colleagues in 1984, that affirmed Montaignier’s finding. According to Montaignier, it was one of these publications, in particular, that “convinced the scientific community that this new retrolentivirus was the cause of AIDS.”</p> <p>This example shows something that is true across the sciences. New discoveries that eventually become accepted as scientific facts can linger for an extended period as mere “claims” while uncertainties are addressed.</p> <p>Critics argue that the scientific uncertainty around the discovery of the AIDS virus was unnecessarily prolonged and cost lives. If moving quickly on yet-to-be-validated evidence is the right approach during a pandemic, note that Fauci and his public health colleagues are currently being attacked for doing exactly that. Public health experts believed at the outset that COVID-19 was like SARS, with transmission most likely to occur late in the course of infection. Hence the guidance that directed the public and health care workers to wear masks when caring for patients already showing symptoms. Mounting evidence of asymptomatic infection eventually proved that COVID-19 transmission was very different from SARS, leading to new masking guidance.</p> <p>When should public health experts act on early, but unvalidated, evidence versus taking the time to iron out uncertainties? While it may look obvious in hindsight, there is no magic formula that can sort out in advance when the better course will have been to slow down and validate versus act on plausible, but still uncertain, claims.</p> <p>Climate scientists would almost certainly never argue their experience in the public eye has been a picnic. But they had one big advantage over those trying to guide the response to a pandemic driven by a novel infectious disease. Climate scientists had decades—as opposed to only weeks or days—to conduct research before they were asked to explain what they knew to the public. In fact, climate scientists did not always expect warming to result from burning fossil fuels. Up until the 1950s, the prevailing wisdom was that the oceans would absorb excess carbon dioxide so that there would be minimal if any warming. Roger Revelle and Hans Seuss, who together discovered the error, both received awards for their research.</p> <p>When a novel infectious disease comes to town, the first cases detected are rarely the actual start of the outbreak. There are no tests to make a positive diagnosis. Some of the suspected cases turn out to have other causes. People who are infected are overlooked. Data collected at the outset is patchy and error-prone. As the public health community pivots to emergency response footing, they begin to collect data more systematically. Even so, new data can rapidly overturn early assumptions. The case definition for COVID-19 was updated almost weekly during the first 10 weeks of the pandemic.</p> <p>Monday morning quarterbacking is easy. Try advising countries on how to manage a growing pandemic while the ground is moving beneath your feet.</p> <p>As the United States’ performance during the COVID-19 pandemic is reviewed, even those who are not engaging in political grandstanding tend to reduce the effort to a scorecard that tallies the times experts were right versus the times they were wrong. Even if the reversals are few in number, they are barely tolerated. We usually give examinations to people after they have had time to learn and master the material. What is the right metric to use for public health experts who are trying to inform us when the answers are still being discovered?</p> <p>Speaking of treasure, I think we were lucky during COVID-19 to have public health experts who were willing to admit mistakes as soon as they were discovered. Things will go markedly worse for us if, during the next pandemic, they are less forthcoming.</p> <p>An earlier version of this article first appeared on MS NOW.</p> <p>Ann Keller, Ph.D., is an associate professor of health politics & policy at UC Berkeley School of Public Health.</p> <p>Many decision makers are not drawing from the relevant findings in well-being research. Here's how to change that.</p> <p>When Americans face complex decisions on immigration, climate change or political candidates, they usually don't consider all of the relevant factors.</p> <p>Election season can make many of us feel anxious and helpless. Here are three ways to protect your well-being without tuning out.</p> <p>Do you embrace a diversity of backgrounds and opinions in others?</p> <p>What does it actually take to put people over politics? Republican and Democrat students discover ways to resist the pull to demean or villainize people with whom they strongly disagree.</p> <p>Discover how writing about our ancestors can strengthen our sense of identity, deepen gratitude, and help us find meaning in our own lives.</p> <p>The Greater Good Science Center studies the psychology, sociology, and neuroscience of well-being, and teaches skills that foster a thriving, resilient, and compassionate society.</p> <p>© 2026 The Greater Good Science Center at the University of California, Berkeley</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/article/item/scientists_admit_mistakes_science_working_fauci_hearings" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://minimalistbaker.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/Gluten-Free-Honey-Cake-15-683x1024.jpg" alt="1-Bowl Honey Almond Snack Cake (Gluten-Free)" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Disclosure: This post may contain affiliate links which provide us a small commission when used for purchase. We're grateful for your support!</p> <p>Honey almond snack cake!? You know you want to jump in on the fun! This GORGEOUS loaf is perfectly moist with a lightly floral flavor and beautiful sponge texture. Bonus? It’s made without gluten or dairy, but no one will know.</p> <p>It’s the perfect cake for afternoon tea, brunch gatherings, and beyond! Just 10 ingredients, 1 bowl, and simple methods (no mixer) required. Let’s bake!</p> <p>This light, fluffy gluten-free honey almond cake is made with 10 simple ingredients:</p> <p>After mixing together your wet ingredients, then adding your dry ingredients, it’s time to pour the batter into a parchment-lined loaf pan. The parchment paper will prevent sticking and make it super easy to remove the cake from the pan.</p> <p>We also think this cake would work beautifully in an 8-inch round cake pan, but it will bake much faster!</p> <p>Top with sliced almonds before baking, then pop that beauty in the oven! After baking and letting the cake cool slightly, we love to add an extra drizzle of honey. Deliciousness awaits, friends!</p> <p>We hope you LOVE this honey almond cake! It’s:FluffyFloralSpongySubtly sweetPerfectly moist& SO delicious!</p> <p>Grab a slice of cake, pour yourself a mug of coffee or tea, kick back, and get your snack on! It would also pair well with Earl Grey Tea, our Lemon Ginger Jasmine Iced Tea, or a Cinnamon Vanilla Dandelion Tea Latte.</p> <p>If you try this recipe, let us know! Leave a comment, rate it, and don’t forget to tag a photo @minimalistbaker on Instagram. Cheers, friends!</p> <p>Tag @minimalistbaker on Instagram and hashtag it #minimalistbaker so we can see all the deliciousness!FacebookTwitterPin It</p> <p>Have a question? Use ctrl+f or ⌘+f on your computer or the "find on page" function on your phone browser to search existing comments! Need help? Check out this tutorial!</p> <p>Can this be made without honey? If so, what would be the substitute?</p> <p>Hi Jessica, perhaps agave or maple syrup, but we haven’t tested with those alternatives. The flavor will vary, especially if using maple. Let us know if you try it out!</p> <p>wow – I absolutely loved this! Incredible flavor and very tender crumb… I can’t believe this combo of pantry ingredients could produce such a fantastic GF cake. And full disclosure – I was kind of winging it with what I had, so I made a version of GF flour with potato starch, white rice flour, sourgum flour and oat flour, and I only had whole almonds so I chopped them roughly for the top. I baked it in my air fryer – a total experiment, and I had to cover it with foil after 10 minutes (did it in an 8×8 pan) – and while it didn’t come out perfectly (it cooked a little unevenly), it was utterly delicious! So moist, with the browned sides and beautifully browned almonds (a benefit of the air fryer, maybe). All to say – this recipe is very adaptable and honestly so so scrumptious. I just had to tell you!</p> <p>We’re so glad you enjoyed it, Ann! Thanks so much for the lovely review and for sharing your modifications. xo</p> <p>Could I use almond meal instead of almond flour? Or would the change in texture be too drastic?</p> <p>Hey Serena! We think it would work, but the flavor and texture might change a bit! Let us know if you try it!</p> <p>Honey almond snack cake looks like the perfect simple bake. Appreciate how approachable the steps stay while still feeling special — trying a small cake for weekend coffee.</p> <p>I made this as written (but with butter) and it is delightful! I love everything about it! Thanks for another great recipe!</p> <p>We’re so glad you enjoyed it, Lisa! Thanks so much for the lovely review. xo</p> <p>Made this and loooove it! Came out really fluffy and delicious. Only modification is brand – I used Earth balance plant butter and Silk protein vegan vanilla yogurt. I also baked slightly longer as the core was still really wet at 45 minutes. Ended up being closer to 55-57mins in my oven. Great recipe, thanks!</p> <p>We’re so glad you enjoyed it, Teya! Thanks so much for sharing. xo</p> <p>I made this and it came out delicious. I was wondering if I could 1/2 cup of applesauce for added moisture?</p> <p>We’re so glad you enjoyed it! Applesauce might make it a bit too dense, but let us know if you do any experimenting!</p> <p>I followed the recipe and I added 1/2 cup unsweetened applesauce. It added a nice flavor (apples go well with honey) and it made it moist. It was a tiny bit more dense, but it helped to maintain the texture throughout the week.</p> <p>We’re so glad you enjoyed it with the applesauce, Susan! Thanks so much for sharing. xo</p> <p>I made this today with flax egg and it came out beautifully.</p> <p>Some specifics: My flax egg was made with aquafaba instead of water (I had some handy from a fresh pot of chickpeas). My flour was a GF flour from my local grocery store’s private label. I baked it in an 8″ round glass cake pan in my toaster oven. My crumb was tender but a little more dense than yours (and darker due to the flax and my blend of flour).</p> <p>We’re so glad the flax egg worked, Sara! Thanks so much for the lovely review and for sharing your modifications. xo</p> <p>Hi! Where do you manage to find Miyoko’s vegan butter? We live in Florida and sadly I haven’t been able to find it at our Whole Foods for almost a year already!! So sad as it has no replacement! Also – I love honey in cakes but stopped using it as heated honey is unhealthy. Would maple work here if I can get the butter?</p> <p>Hey there! Sprouts usually has Miyoko’s if Whole Food’s doesn’t. You could also use another vegan butter here. We have learned that heated honey isn’t necessarily unhealthy, heating it just get’s rid of some of the benefits of raw honey. It’s still safe to bake with! We’re not sure if maple syrup would work, but let us know if you try it!</p> <p>Sounds like another great recipe! Do you think I make it in muffin tins instead? How long would the bake time be then? Thank you! /Mattis</p> <p>Hey Mattis! We haven’t tried the recipe as muffins, but we think it would definitely work! We would suggest starting with a 23 minute bake time and then checking them every 3-5 minutes after until done! Let us know if you try it.</p> <p>This recipe is perfect for Rosh Hashanah shana! I can’t wait to make it for the high holidays. Do you think that I could add chunks of apple or decorate it with sliced apples on top?</p> <p>We’re so glad, Caryn! We’re not sure exactly how the cake would react to the apple, but our suggestion would be if you do add chunks to the cake to coat them in a little flour first to make sure they don’t sink to the bottom! Then you can fold the flour coated apples into the cake right before you add the batter to the pan. They might work on top of the cake, but we would suggest watching it while it bakes to make sure they don’t burn! Let us know if you try it either way!</p> <p>I think I’m going to try subbing sourdough starter for yogurt–I’ll report back with results!</p> <p>Get our copy of FAN FAVORITES featuring 20 of our most loved, highly-rated recipes!</p> <p>Our FREE 49-Page Fan Favorites e-Book has 20 recipes we think you’ll LOVE! Please enable JavaScript in your browser to complete this form.Email *WebsiteSubmit</p> <p>Our FREE 49-Page Fan Favorites e-Book has 20 recipes we think you’ll LOVE! Please enable JavaScript in your browser to complete this form.Email *EmailSubmit</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://minimalistbaker.com/honey-almond-snack-cake/" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9526"> <h2>#9526. Fall Freezer Meals #2</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://pinchofyum.com/tachyon/Fall-Freezer-Meals-2-1.jpg" alt="Fall Freezer Meals #2" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>These Fall Freezer Meals have been SO helpful for us. The prep is shockingly easy!</p> <p>Published by Lindsay Ostrom on October 14, 2026</p> <p>A few months ago, I discovered what feels like a little life hack.</p> <p>I started spending an hour each month getting a few meals prepped for the month ahead. We’re talking just assembling stuff for my favorite recipes into bags and freezing it!</p> <p>And I can’t tell you how much this system makes me feel like I have my life together! It’s the best.</p> <p>The recipes this month are absolute family favorites for fall!</p> <p>And they all have cook times for Crockpot, Instant Pot, and stovetop methods. 🙂</p> <p>Hope these help make your life easier this month like they have for us!</p> <p>Everything you need is right on them. I print the cards out and attach them to the bags so I don’t have to use my phone at all for the prep or cooking.</p> <p>For the streusel: mix 4 tablespoons melted butter, 1/3 cup brown sugar, and 3/4 cup flour into small crumbles.</p> <p>Spray a muffin tin with avocado oil. Fill tins two-thirds of the way full with batter; top with streusel.</p> <p>Store muffins in an airtight container or bag in the freezer (or fridge). To reheat from frozen, microwave 45-60 seconds.</p> <p>Remove chicken from the sauce and shred. Blend sauce until smooth. Add chicken back in. Serve in tortillas with all the taco fixings you want!</p> <p>Add 1-2 cups heavy cream and 1-2 cups chicken broth (as needed). To thicken: whisk 2 tbsp. cornstarch with 2 tbsp. cold water; add and simmer.</p> <p>Whisk 1 1/2 tbsp. cornstarch in 1 1/2 tbsp. cold water; add to bubbling pot and let simmer until slightly thickened.</p> <p>Stir in 2 cups of fresh spinach and fresh cilantro just before serving.</p> <p>Serve with rice and chili crisp. I also love this with cucumber salad (thinly sliced cucumber and red onion, tossed with vinegar, avocado oil, salt, and sugar).</p> <p>I’m Lindsay and I ♡ FOOD. I used to be a teacher, and now making food and writing about it online is my full-time job. I love talking with people about food, and I'm so glad you're here.</p> <p>Did you make a recipe? Tag @pinchofyum on Instagram so we can find you!</p> <p>Your email address will not be published. Required fields are marked *</p> <p>Sign me up for recipes, please!All the food, right to your inbox (and a FREE ecookbook, too!).</p> <p>I love this idea! Spending just an hour preparing freezer meals for the month sounds like such a practical way to make busy weekdays easier. The variety is great too, especially having options like chicken tinga tacos, wild rice soup, and chickpea curry with different cooking methods. I also appreciate the printable labels and grocery lists because they make meal prep much more organized. These recipes would be especially helpful for anyone balancing a busy schedule with home-cooked meals. Thanks for sharing!</p> <p>Very interesting post. Just thinking about the option to add to instant pot. How would that work? You put everything frozen (without any other unfrozen liquid), put the lid and select the number of minutes? So everything will thaw in the IP before it pressurized?</p> <p>Hi there, how long do these recipes stay good for in the freezer? I would like to have these as back ups. Thank you.</p> <p>Love your recipes! I love curry and the recipe for Chickpea curry looks fabulous, but, my husband is not a chickpea for protein kind of guy. Can I use chicken or shrimp instead and how much would I use?</p> <p>Can you clarify the liquid added to the chicken and wild rice soup? I’m reading 5 cups broth for cooking and then another 2.5 to finish with 2 cups cream, is that right?</p> <p>Hello! Yes, it is another 1-2 cups of broth added, as needed, with the cream. You can adjust depending on how thick you like your soup.</p> <p>Thank you so much for sharing these wonderful ideas! I love your recipes. For the Chicken Wild Rice Soup- Would a combination of Heavy Cream and Whole Milk work here like in the original blog post? What ratio do you think would be best if I did that? Thank you!</p> <p>I love both the original bechamel (butter / flour / milk) method, and the heavy cream method! 🙂 For this version, I opted for the heavy cream just because it’s easier to put onto the small cards. But the bechamel is great and it will get a bit thicker than just using cream. If you want that version, I’d just make the bechamel and add it at the end, using the same quantities as in this post: https://pinchofyum.com/crockpot-chicken-wild-rice-soup</p> <p>Hi there! Always wondering about the prep for chicken thighs, how much do you trim the fat and gristle from them? It takes me so long and I’m always wondering if it’s worth doing.</p> <p>Unless it’s a big piece of fat that you can easily cut off, you can definitely skip the trimming.</p> <p>Love the recipes I have tried! Going to try the freezer prep soup and muffins. Thanks for the recipes</p> <p>Can you use chicken breast instead of chicken thighs in the tinga tacos?</p> <p>Yep! I prefer thighs because they stay a bit juicier, but chicken breasts can absolutely work. 🙂 I would pull them out of the sauce when they’re done and really kind of -chop them into shreddy chunks rather than straight shred them – maybe it’s just me, but I find that sometimes the shredding with chicken breasts can get a bit stringy.</p> <p>Hi Lindsay, Thank you so much for all of your great recipes and ideas! I really appreciate all the hard work.</p> <p>You’re so welcome! I really have enjoyed doing these for myself these last few months, so it’s fun to share them!</p> <p>Lindsay – LOVE your recipes! Question about the freezer meals. There are a couple that you say you freeze the chicken separately but on the Chicken Wild Rice Soup it looks like you put the chicken in the same bag with everything. Can you please clarify for me? Thank you!!</p> <p>Yes! 🙂 Short answer – you can put the chicken in the bag, or add it later. Either can work. Long answer – With the first batch I did in September, I left the chicken out and added it at the time of cooking (and I wrote that into those recipe cards). I liked how it cooked, but I found it was a little bit inconvenient because I didn’t always have chicken on hand when I needed it. So for round two / the set of recipes in this post, I decided to include the chicken in the bag. All these recipes now have chicken going into the bag with everything else, and all the cook times are listed with that in mind.</p> <p>These were so easy and awesome. I prepped one of everything for my friend who just had a major surgery, and another batch for my family. I hope you keep coming out with these!</p> <p>Love that you are sharing these meals with others!</p> <p>Any replacement ideas for chipotles in adobo? Worried too spicy for the kids.</p> <p>Freezer crockpot meals are great for camping. Prep is pretty much done. Put them in the crockpot and enjoy after a day of hiking and fun. Delicious!</p> <p>I’ve been freezer cooking for years and have seen nearly all the websites on the topic.</p> <p>Yours are simply THE BEST label layout I’ve ever come across! Kudos to you!</p> <p>Thank you so much Jerri! I work on these freezer meals with Jenna on our team, and the two of us really try to make them feel as user friendly as possible! 🙂</p> <p>I'm a former 4th grade teacher, now full time blogger. My husband Bjork and I live in Minnesota. Favorite things include my camera, lake days, and dark chocolate.</p> <p>Get a Free eCookbook with our top 25 recipes.</p> <p>The eBook includes our most popular 25 recipes in a beautiful, easy to download format. Enter your email and we'll send it right over!</p> <p>Get a Free eCookbook with our top 25 recipes.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://pinchofyum.com/fall-freezer-meals-2" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9525"> <h2>#9525. TikTok Mental Health Advice Has A Serious Problem Many Fail To Spot (M)</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://www.spring.org.uk/images/tiktok-1.jpg" alt="TikTok Mental Health Advice Has A Serious Problem Many Fail To Spot (M)" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Young people know TikTok can be unreliable, but its design makes it surprisingly difficult to separate useful advice from misinformation.</p> <p>Young people know TikTok can be unreliable, but its design makes it surprisingly difficult to separate useful advice from misinformation.</p> <p>• Read members-only articles • Adverts removed • Cancel at any time • 14 day money-back guarantee for new members</p> <p>Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://www.spring.org.uk/2026/10/tiktok-advice.php" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9524"> <h2>#9524. Cheesy Vegan Enchilada Skillet (30 Minutes!)</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://minimalistbaker.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Cheesy-Vegan-Black-Bean-Enchilada-Skillet-9.jpg" alt="Cheesy Vegan Enchilada Skillet (30 Minutes!)" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Disclosure: This post may contain affiliate links which provide us a small commission when used for purchase. We're grateful for your support!</p> <p>Everything you love about enchiladas, minus the fuss! This super flavorful, cheesy vegan enchilada skillet comes together in about 30 minutes with simple methods, minimal dishes, and no need to fill or roll tortillas.</p> <p>This easy, nourishing dish features tender cubed sweet potato or winter squash, fiber- & protein-rich black beans, and a rich red enchilada sauce. Everything gets simmered in 1 pan and topped with a melty cashew “cheese” that makes it SUPER satisfying and delicious!</p> <p>It’s believed that enchiladas may have originated from a similar Mayan dish called papadzules. But the first written recipe for enchiladas was in an 1831 cookbook called El Cocinero mexicano. Typically, enchiladas are made with meat, seafood, beans, cheese, potatoes, or vegetables stuffed in corn tortillas and topped with enchilada sauce.</p> <p>Our “inspired-by” enchilada skillet has all the flavors of classic enchiladas, but it’s vegan, and instead of rolling the filling in tortillas, we slice the tortillas and cook everything together in one pan on the stovetop!</p> <p>This 1-pan, 30-minute vegan enchilada skillet begins with a base of sautéed vegetables — onion, garlic, sweet potato, and poblano pepper. The veggies are flexible here, so feel free to experiment! We love kabocha squash for a fall variation and have found green bell peppers work well when poblanos aren’t available. We also think butternut squash would be nice, as would greens such as kale or spinach.</p> <p>Once the onions are very tender and the squash and peppers are just beginning to soften, we stir in black beans + corn tortillas that have been sliced into strips.</p> <p>Next comes the final ingredient in the skillet portion of this dish (hello, simple + flavorful!): red enchilada sauce. We love the bold flavor of our homemade enchilada sauce (and usually have it stocked in the freezer), but this recipe also works well with store-bought enchilada sauce.</p> <p>And lastly, it just wouldn’t be enchiladas without: the CHEESE! More specifically, a flavorful cashew “cheese” sauce inspired by our fan favorite Cheesy Vegan Pizza Beans. It’s made by blending up cashews, water, lime juice, garlic, tapioca starch, and sea salt. When poured over the enchilada skillet and covered with a lid, the heat and tapioca starch do their magic, creating a melty, cheesy layer! Total swoon!</p> <p>We highly recommend trying the cashew “cheese” sauce, even if you’re not vegan or dairy-free! It’s super easy and takes this dish to a whole new level. However, this enchilada skillet is also delicious with shredded vegan or dairy cheese (such as pepper jack).</p> <p>We think you’ll LOVE this recipe! It’s:SmokySpicySuper flavorfulSatisfyingVersatileQuick & easy to make& SO delicious!</p> <p>This dish is hearty and amazing as a standalone quick meal for weeknights! It would also pair well with our Smoky Shredded Tofu Taco “Meat” or 1-Pan Mexican Shredded Chicken for a higher-protein option. Or, for more veggies, try it with our Crunchy Jicama Slaw or Quick Citrusy Cabbage Slaw.</p> <p>If you try this recipe, let us know! Leave a comment, rate it, and don’t forget to tag a photo @minimalistbaker on Instagram. Cheers, friends!</p> <p>Tag @minimalistbaker on Instagram and hashtag it #minimalistbaker so we can see all the deliciousness!FacebookTwitterPin It</p> <p>Have a question? Use ctrl+f or ⌘+f on your computer or the "find on page" function on your phone browser to search existing comments! Need help? Check out this tutorial!</p> <p>One of the best things I’ve made in a while!! I love how the cheesy sauce solidified on the skillet! 🔥🤤 I subbed the beans for vegan beef and tapioca flour for cornstarch.</p> <p>Whoop! We’re so glad you loved this one, Elizabeth. Thank you for the lovely review and for sharing your modifications! xo</p> <p>Made this tonight for the first time and it was delicious! I’ll be adding this to the dinner menu this winter. I was a bit worried that the cashew cheese was going to be too runny, but sure enough, after adding it to the skillet and covering for 5min, this creamy cheesy goodness was perfect!</p> <p>I didn’t have any corn tortillas, so we left those out and had corn chips on the side. Thank you for this yummy 1-ppt meal!</p> <p>Thank you for the lovely review, Taylor! We’re so glad you enjoyed the recipe and will be adding it into your winter dinner rotation! xo</p> <p>Well that was delightful. Very different for me – my first time buying enchilada sauce. And first time making a cashew cheese. It took more time than indicated – all that fine chopping – but was absolutely delicious. A great one pot meal – thanks!</p> <p>Thank you for sharing your experience, Kate! We’re so happy to hear you enjoyed the dish! Sorry it took longer than expected. xo</p> <p>the “cheese” sauce on top isn’t thickening and is just remaining in a water-like consistency. troubleshooting ideas?</p> <p>Hi! Sorry the hear it’s giving you some trouble. A few ideas: 1) Is it possible the tapioca starch got left out? 2) Is the enchilada layer extra watery? 3) Did you give it a full 5 minutes? You can even keep going past that – it should help. 4) Did you soak your cashews? If so, did you use slightly less water when blending? We hope one of those ideas helps!</p> <p>This was easy and delicious. As the directions say, since my squash was cut a little larger I had to steam longer. I used corn starch instead of tapioca starch and it worked! This one will be on repeat at our house.</p> <p>Thank you for sharing your experience, Alicia! We’re so glad you enjoyed this dish and will be making it again.</p> <p>Yum! I love pizza beans and made it not too long ago.</p> <p>This looks like a nice Mexican twist that is a must-try!</p> <p>It SO is! We’re excited to hear what you think of this one!</p> <p>Yay! We’re so excited to hear what you think, Gina! xo</p> <p>Hi Chana, zucchini will add more moisture which may dilute the flavor, but you could try it! We would suggest chopping it into small cubes and adding in place of the poblano pepper. Let us know if you try it out!</p> <p>This looks so good! Can you recommend any substitutions for tapioca starch? I have an intolerance.</p> <p>Hi Christine, we would suggest trying arrowroot, or possibly corn starch. Let us know if you try it out!</p> <p>Get our copy of FAN FAVORITES featuring 20 of our most loved, highly-rated recipes!</p> <p>Our FREE 49-Page Fan Favorites e-Book has 20 recipes we think you’ll LOVE! Please enable JavaScript in your browser to complete this form.Email *CommentSubmit</p> <p>Our FREE 49-Page Fan Favorites e-Book has 20 recipes we think you’ll LOVE! Do You Compare Yourself to Your Partner? It’s Not All Bad</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://ggsc.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/assets/images/couple_partner_comparison_-_abcdef_-_0a21b39134b316e51cdc0dd96c5e6bca3c0093e9-fb_-_abcdef_-_94b15742ccdfc3b16fb1fe35872167fe8d42c35d.webp" alt="Do You Compare Yourself to Your Partner? It’s Not All Bad" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.</p> <p>Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education</p> <p>After venturing through the wasteland of modern dating, it would be natural to harbor disdain for social comparison. Dating apps require you to stand out, which means you can’t just be yourself; you need to sell yourself as more appealing than the 50,000 sexy singles in your area. Putting yourself on display and knowing you’re being compared to others can feel exhausting. But once you’ve swiped right, matched, and established a lasting romantic relationship, surely the social comparisons are all in the rearview mirror…right?</p> <p>That couldn’t be further from the truth. Research suggests we compare ourselves to romantic partners more than anyone else in our lives—on average several times per day. In my own studies, I’ve endeavored to unpack these daily partner comparisons to understand: What kinds of people make partner comparisons, and why? The answer, it seems, depends on the type of comparisons partners are making: either based on our unique abilities, or on the opinions we hold. The good news: Comparisons can offer a learning opportunity and even bring us closer together as partners.</p> <p>Many partner comparisons revolve around who is better at a given activity—also known as “ability-based comparisons.” These comparisons can range from trivial (Who’s the better bowler?) to weighty (Who’s the better parent?).</p> <p>In my latest study with collaborators Robin Edelstein and Stephen Garcia, we studied patterns in who makes more of these ability-based comparisons. We surveyed over 1,100 U.S. adults in romantic relationships, asking them questions about how regularly they compare themselves to their partners. For instance, one question asked them, “To what extent do you pay a lot of attention to how you do things relative to how your significant other does things?” Participants also completed measures of self-esteem, relationship quality, and demographics.</p> <p>The results were clear: People who were younger, those with lower self-esteem, and those in shorter and less satisfying relationships were particularly likely to make ability-based comparisons. Men in relationships with men also reported making more of these comparisons than any other gender pairing, but we only surveyed 37 men in same-gender relationships, so take this finding with a grain of salt.</p> <p>A second type of comparison involves comparing judgments and attitudes—known as “opinion-based comparisons.” In these comparisons, people evaluate their own opinions by comparing with those of their partners. For instance, before enthusiastically locking in a major purchase, a partner might wonder, “Would my partner consider this a good deal, too?” Similar considerations may arise in the contexts of voting, child care, or anywhere judgments lead to decisions.</p> <p>When it came to who was most prone to making opinion-based comparisons, our results flipped: These were most common among people in longer and more satisfying relationships.</p> <p>Taken together, these individual characteristics paint two portraits of people who frequently compare themselves to their partners.</p> <p>The first portrait is that of a young, insecure partner who is in a newer relationship and unsure whether that relationship will work out. Think Bella Swan from Twilight who worries endlessly about whether Edward is too good for her. And, indeed, when we asked participants why they made partner comparisons, two of their motives included assessing equity and predicting the relationship’s trajectory. For instance, participants grappled with questions like, “Am I doing for her as she is doing for me?”</p> <p>The second portrait is that of someone in a long-term relationship who respects the knowledge and expertise of their partner and seeks to harness it as a tool for growth and decision making. For this one, think Leslie Knope from Parks and Rec who regularly compares her own judgments to those of her long-term work wife, Ann Perkins, as a means to make better decisions. This theme, too, emerged from our participants. For instance, one participant lovingly wrote about how his partner outshines him in most areas, and this dynamic continually inspires him to grow.</p> <p>Yet partner comparison isn’t limited to these two portraits. Whereas these portraits describe those who compare most frequently, we found most people make some comparisons sometimes. What motivates occasional comparers?</p> <p>The two most common motives for partner comparison were striving to gain a deeper understanding of oneself and one’s partner. With respect to self-evaluation, one participant shared that they compare regularly to their partner because comparison helps them benchmark their progress toward goals. Want to know if your cooking class has paid off? One of the best ways to evaluate your growth is to see if your latest dish can delight your family in the same way that your partner’s cooking always does.</p> <p>This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.</p> <p>Partner comparisons can also help us understand our partners’ quirks, what we call partner evaluation. For instance, one participant shared how she compares her upbringing to that of her partner, which helps her understand why her partner thinks, feels, and behaves so differently than she does.</p> <p>It’s no secret that social comparison can sting. No parent wants to hear, “I like Mom better,” and no newlywed wants to hear, “How did you land such a catch?” We find in our studies that partner comparisons are often involuntarily thrust upon people who would have preferred not to be compared. It can be true what they say, “Comparison is the thief of joy.”</p> <p>But comparison does more than push our emotional buttons. Partner comparisons help us assess our relationship and calibrate our behavior, such as how we divide household labor. They allow us to make important decisions, like who should take ownership over responsibilities. They serve as sources of growth, and they teach us about ourselves and our partners.</p> <p>Comparing yourself to your partner isn’t necessarily a sign that something’s wrong. Rather, partner comparison can be a handy strategy for making sense of your social world. The key is to use it as a tool that stays in its place, rather than letting it undermine your self-worth or relationship.</p> <p>Serena D’souza contributed to this article.</p> <p>Zachary Reese, Ph.D., is an assistant professor of psychology at the University of San Francisco where he directs the Love and Communication Lab. He received his undergraduate degree in psychology from Goucher College in 2016 and his Ph.D. in social psychology from the University of Michigan in 2022.</p> <p>Sending reels on social media may seem frivolous or distracting, but it actually functions as a form of relationship maintenance.</p> <p>New research is exploring how our brains translate other people's actions into the experience of feeling loved.</p> <p>Our contributors award our annual "Greater Goodies" to the TV shows that might help you be your best self.</p> <p>What does it actually take to put people over politics? Republican and Democrat students discover ways to resist the pull to demean or villainize people with whom they strongly disagree.</p> <p>Discover how writing about our ancestors can strengthen our sense of identity, deepen gratitude, and help us find meaning in our own lives.</p> <p>The Greater Good Science Center studies the psychology, sociology, and neuroscience of well-being, and teaches skills that foster a thriving, resilient, and compassionate society.</p> <p>© 2026 The Greater Good Science Center at the University of California, Berkeley</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/article/item/do_you_compare_yourself_to_your_partner_its_not_all_bad" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9522"> <h2>#9522. No-Bake Cranberry Orange Bliss Bites</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://minimalistbaker.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/No-Bake-Cranberry-Bliss-Bar-Bites-8.jpg" alt="No-Bake Cranberry Orange Bliss Bites" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Disclosure: This post may contain affiliate links which provide us a small commission when used for purchase. We're grateful for your support!</p> <p>Cozy, bright, and bursting with holiday flavor — these Cranberry Orange Bliss Bites are the perfect little treat when holiday baking season is in full swing and you’re out of time and energy. Inspired by Starbucks’ Bliss Bars, they pack the tart-sweet magic of cranberries and fresh orange zest into tender, no-bake bites you can whip up in minutes!</p> <p>Even better? They’re vegan, gluten-free, and require zero baking — making them a lifesaver during the busy holiday season. A drizzle of white chocolate (or creamy coconut butter) makes them extra festive, but they’re just as delicious on their own. Let’s make bliss bites!</p> <p>Besides tasting absolutely magical, these bliss bites get their name because they’re inspired by the legendary Bliss Bars from Starbucks (IYKYK!). The Starbucks bars have a chewy blondie base with cream cheese frosting, cranberries, white chocolate, and orange zest — total swoon!</p> <p>The addition of orange juice + zest and dried cranberries kick things up a notch and sends them into Bliss Bar territory!</p> <p>The final touch is an optional drizzle of melted white chocolate chips, coconut butter, or our favorite — a mix of the two! While the white chocolate creates a thicker, sweeter, and more decadent frosting, the coconut butter creates a drippier texture and adds a more pronounced coconut flavor that we enjoy. The combination is the best of both worlds!</p> <p>We hope you LOVE these bites! They’re:ZestyBrightSweet with pops of tartnessDecadent yet wholesomeQuick + easy to make& SO delicious!</p> <p>These are the perfect little treat to make during the fall and winter months. They’ve got you covered whether you want something on hand to satisfy sweet cravings during the work week or need a quick healthier dessert to bring to a gathering.</p> <p>If you try this recipe, let us know! Leave a comment, rate it, and don’t forget to tag a photo @minimalistbaker on Instagram. Cheers, friends!</p> <p>Tag @minimalistbaker on Instagram and hashtag it #minimalistbaker so we can see all the deliciousness!FacebookTwitterPin It</p> <p>Have a question? Use ctrl+f or ⌘+f on your computer or the "find on page" function on your phone browser to search existing comments! Need help? Check out this tutorial!</p> <p>Hiya! I am wondering if you might have a grain free substitute for the oatmeal? My husband and I are both grain free. He has Celiac and I am Paleo due to auto-immune issues, and Cranberry orange is our favorite combo that we miss, and this just sounds heavenly and treat like.</p> <p>Hi Wendy, we would suggest trying a lesser amount of coconut flour (maybe 1/4 cup?). Let us know if you try it out!</p> <p>I have been recently enjoying making some of your energy and bliss bites as it feels like an accessible form of sweetness and energy for a snack to keep us going through the day! I was soooooo stoked to see this version in my inbox! (one of the best coffee shop produced dessert bar for sure and one of my fave flavour profiles this time of year!)</p> <p>Will be trying very soon, though I am thinking of blitzing the white chocolate slightly and folding them in! Will report back.</p> <p>Aw, we’re so happy to hear you’ve been enjoying snacking on our energy bites, Dev! We agree – it’s hard to beat the deliciousness of those Starbucks bars and the tart-sweet flavor of cranberry orange is so lovely this time of year. Excited to hear what you think of this version! xo</p> <p>If I want to share these at work, will they soften again once they’re out of the refrigerator?</p> <p>Hi Kathy, Yes, they will soften a bit at room temperature due to the coconut oil, unless perhaps the room is super cold!</p> <p>For zero coconut flavor, you can use refined coconut oil and white chocolate for the frosting!</p> <p>Hi Tasie, we don’t think they would bake super well due to the ratio of ingredients here, but let us know if you try it!</p> <p>Get our copy of FAN FAVORITES featuring 20 of our most loved, highly-rated recipes!</p> <p>Our FREE 49-Page Fan Favorites e-Book has 20 recipes we think you’ll LOVE! Does β‑Blocker Use Increase Depression Risk?</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://www.psychiatryadvisor.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/8/2022/01/pillsg730138337_1448007-e1656645198731.jpg" alt="Does β‑Blocker Use Increase Depression Risk?" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>The association between β-blocker use and depression was investigated in a population-based observational study recently published in the journal Drug Safety.</p> <p>While depression is often cited as an adverse effect of β-blocker use, there is limited evidence supporting this causal relationship. To better understand the association between beta blockers and the risk of new-onset depression, the study authors analyzed data from the UK population-based Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) GOLD database.</p> <p>“We identifed patients aged 18-80 years with an incident depression diagnosis between 2000 and 2016, and matched controls, and estimated the risk (odds ratio [OR]) of depression in association with use of β-blockers,” the study authors explained.</p> <p>Findings of the analysis revealed an increased risk of developing depression among short-term users of β-blockers compared with no use at all (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.91; 95% CI, 1.72-2.12).</p> <p>Among short-term users, increased risk of depression was mainly restricted to patients with a neuropsychiatric disorder taking propranolol (aOR 6.33, 95% CI 5.16–7.76).  Patients on propranolol for a cardiovascular indication were found to be at slightly elevated risk of depression (aOR 1.44, 95% CI 1.14–1.82). Apart from propranolol, no other lipophilic β-blocker or hydrophilic β-blocker was found to increase the risk of depression.</p> <p>Additionally, no association was observed between long-term use of β-blockers and the risk of depression (aOR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.85-0.94).</p> <p>“Our findings suggest that the reported association between use of β-blockers and depression may not be causal but rather a result of protopathic bias,” the study authors concluded.</p> <p>Bornand D, Reinau D, Jick SS, Meier CR. β‑blockers and the risk of depression: A matched case–control study. Drug Safety. Published online January 19, 2022. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40264-021-01140-5.</p> <p>Psychiatry Advisor, a trusted source of medical news and feature content for healthcare providers, offers clinicians insight into the latest research to inform clinical practice and improve patient outcomes.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://www.psychiatryadvisor.com/home/topics/mood-disorders/depressive-disorder/does-%ce%b2%e2%80%91blocker-use-increase-depression-risk/" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9520"> <h2>#9520. How Your Imagination Can Work for You or Against You</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://ggsc.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/assets/images/how_imagination_works_in_the_brain_-_abcdef_-_0a21b39134b316e51cdc0dd96c5e6bca3c0093e9-fb_-_abcdef_-_94b15742ccdfc3b16fb1fe35872167fe8d42c35d.jpg" alt="How Your Imagination Can Work for You or Against You" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.</p> <p>Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education</p> <p>I have a pretty vivid imagination, sometimes for the good, sometimes not. I love it when it helps me to create new stories or songs, or when I can daydream about fun times ahead. But it can also lead to fear or worry, like when I imagine something terrible befalling the people or places I love.</p> <p>Is there some way to nurture the positive aspects of imagination while minimizing the problematic? According to Cassandra Vieten, director of research at the Arthur C. Clarke Center for Human Imagination, there is. In her new book, Imagine That, she explains imagination’s importance in our everyday lives—a way to understand our past, navigate the present, and explore future possibilities. If we learn more about its inner workings, she argues, we can use it more consciously and deliberately to create the kind of life we want.</p> <p>“Imagination is something we all possess, something we can all practice, for free and with equal opportunity,” says Vieten. “When someone develops this capacity, they gain something almost magical: the ability to see multiple futures simultaneously and navigate toward the preferred ones.”</p> <p>Many of us tend to conflate imagination with creativity, thinking that being able to imagine new ideas is the same as bringing them to fruition. While the two may indeed be related, this is far too limited a view of what imagination can be, writes Vieten.</p> <p>“Imagination is an essential, foundational capacity that allows us to simulate reality and transcend it to explore possibilities beyond the known,” she says.</p> <p>In our everyday lives, imagination is what helps us make predictions as well as come up with novel (or creative) ideas. For example, we might imagine how stopping for a coffee on our way to work will help us focus (simulation imagination, based on past experience). But we might also use our imagination to transcend what’s known and come up with a totally new innovation or product idea once we arrive at the office (generative imagination).</p> <p>“Imagination weaves throughout the fabric of our cognitive, sensory, and relational lives—you are constantly speculating, visualizing, rehearsing, wondering,” she writes.</p> <p>These types of imagination show up differently in the brain, writes Vieten. Simulation is primarily centered in the default mode network (DMN), a part of the brain that remains active when we aren’t engaging in a specific task. The DMN is where we tend to mull over future interactions, plans, or options, often subconsciously (or even unconsciously).</p> <p>Generative imagination, on the other hand, comes by freeing ourselves from the DMN’s limitations (or, some would say, tyranny). If we can get out of the everyday chatter and let our minds truly wander freely around disparate parts of the brain, making new neural connections, we have a better chance of generating something truly unique.</p> <p>“Rather than simulating or iterating, comparing and contrasting, generative imagination is focused on combining, reconfiguring, or transcending existing knowledge to generate novel outputs,” writes Vieten.</p> <p>Either way, imagination isn’t frivolous, she writes; it’s important for our everyday functioning as well as creative self-expression. It helps us solve problems, while also expanding possibilities of what could be, giving us “the gift of wonder, whimsy, and surprise, the whoas and the wows of our lives,” she writes.</p> <p>Imagination can sometimes be problematic, though. For example, we might imagine that our spouse is mad at us and worry about what might happen when she gets home from work when, actually, she’s not mad at all. This can cause us needless worry, not to mention potentially trigger a fight.</p> <p>We can also imagine that other people are unpleasant or even dangerous based on untested biases. These can be formed in part via our imagination, which tries to prepare us for unknown encounters, often behind the scenes at an unconscious level.</p> <p>“We regularly imagine entire narratives, scenes, and interactions without intending to or even knowing we’re doing it,” writes Vieten.</p> <p>Our imagination is often busy filling in the missing parts of our memories and perceptions, which are by nature incomplete. Memories, rather than being etched in our minds, are recreated (and often changed) each time they’re recalled. Similarly, we can’t perceive everything at once, so our imagination completes the picture for us, adding interpretations, too. This means it’s easy to corrupt memories or miss details of a situation—which can sometimes lead to problems (think eyewitness accounts of crimes, for example).</p> <p>Understanding these darker sides of imagination can help us tame them somewhat, says Vieten. “You can practice bringing greater attention to what you are imagining, recognize it as imagination, and decide whether it holds useful information, is irrelevant, or is actually causing harm.”</p> <p>While the book covers the neuroscience behind imagination, it’s also about how to harness our imagination more effectively. Your personal imagination style may depend, in part, on your genetics (such as neurodiversity), culture, and life experiences. Understanding this can help you figure out where you might want to try moving the needle one way or the other.</p> <p>To assess your own imaginative strengths and weaknesses, here are some key imagination modes Vieten outlines in her book.</p> <p>1. Receptiveness. “How willing you are to imagine—and how receptive you are to whatever bubbles up.” If you are high in receptivity, you may find it easy to do guided visualizations, for example; if low in receptivity, you may be less willing to imagine unknown scenarios.</p> <p>2. Presence. How much do you embody your imagined experiences? If you tend to be absorbed, immersed, and emotionally involved in imagined scenarios, you’re high in presence; if you tend to observe these imaginings from a distance, you’re less so.</p> <p>3. Embellishment. “How vivid, detailed, and elaborate people make their imaginings.” Those high in embellishment can imagine intricate scenarios with much more detail, clarity, nuance, and complexity. Those low in embellishment might be more “big picture” folks, who may not be able to conjure up details as much.</p> <p>4. Originality. How much your imagination is fueled by what is or could be, based on reality, versus how much it veers from that and is based more on fantasy and novelty.</p> <p>5. Temporality. How much your imagination is associated with time (in other words, assessing the past or projecting into the future) versus how much it is agnostic around time (not based on any particular time). (Vieten admits the science on this mode is not completely settled, but says there appear to be some differences in how people engage with time while imagining.)</p> <p>Each of these modes has pros and cons, she argues. For example, being high in receptivity may mean you’re more cognitively flexible and open to new experiences, but can also mean you’re overly compliant and easily manipulated. Similarly, the upside of being high in originality is that it can fuel advancements in art and science, though it can lead to boredom with everyday life.</p> <p>Considering my own strengths and weaknesses, I noticed that I seem to be high in receptivity and embodiment, but low in embellishment and originality (and mixed when it comes to temporality). Recognizing this makes me think about paying more attention to details in my environment and playing around with more fantastical ideas, especially if I’m wanting to fuel my creativity.</p> <p>To that end, Vieten provides avenues for stretching our imagination in different ways. Some ideas for accessing different aspects of imagination deliberately include rehearsing something before doing it, brainstorming ideas, engaging all of our senses when imagining something, reframing an idea from a different perspective, and freewriting.</p> <p>Vieten also suggests creating environments conducive to being more spontaneously creative. Setting time aside to daydream, being in solitude where your mind can wander, taking walks in the woods to de-stress, or, possibly, taking psychedelic drugs (in a safe, controlled environment) can all help us disengage our DMN and allow creative thoughts to enter more freely.</p> <p>“One of the key ways to make imagination welcome is to remove the practical pressures of the world,” she writes.</p> <p>Imagine That is full of suggestions for unleashing your imagination, all based on the emerging science of imagination that Vieten and her colleagues (and others) are exploring.</p> <p>But while the book reads mostly as a self-help guide, there’s also an important message about why using our imagination is beneficial to society as a whole. Too many of us are experiencing the hopelessness and despair that come with being alive right now, writes Vieten. It’s too easy to get lost in the negative news cycles and focus on all of the problems in the world, making it more difficult to imagine anything better for our collective future.</p> <p>Learning how to engage our imagination more readily can create a sense of hope in our current situation. Not only can it bring more joy and aliveness to our individual lives, countering malaise, it can also lead to new ways of collaborating with others and innovating to solve societal problems, thereby providing a better life for everyone.</p> <p>“So many of the issues facing us locally and globally are rooted in our collective inability to imagine new solutions, alternative futures, creative pathways forward that could build a world that promotes thriving for all,” writes Vieten. “My deepest hope is that [you] take a deeper dive into the science, the practice, and the magic of imagination and [see] how it can re-enchant your life and our world.”</p> <p>Jill Suttie, Psy.D., is Greater Good’s former book review editor and now serves as a staff writer and contributing editor for the magazine. She received her doctorate of psychology from the University of San Francisco in 1998 and was a psychologist in private practice before coming to Greater Good.</p> <p>A father of three reflects on how becoming a parent taught him about love and helped him grow as a human being.</p> <p>While drug-induced mystical experiences can have benefits, research suggests they may not be enough to create lasting change.</p> <p>Despite how advanced robots have become, getting them to feel the way humans do is an incredibly complex challenge.</p> <p>What does it actually take to put people over politics? Republican and Democrat students discover ways to resist the pull to demean or villainize people with whom they strongly disagree.</p> <p>Discover how writing about our ancestors can strengthen our sense of identity, deepen gratitude, and help us find meaning in our own lives.</p> <p>The Greater Good Science Center studies the psychology, sociology, and neuroscience of well-being, and teaches skills that foster a thriving, resilient, and compassionate society.</p> <p>© 2026 The Greater Good Science Center at the University of California, Berkeley</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/article/item/how_your_imagination_can_work_for_you_or_against_you" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9519"> <h2>#9519. Easy Seasoned Pretzels</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p><h2><a href="https://sallysbakingaddiction.com/moms-seasoned-pretzels/">Easy Seasoned Pretzels</a></h2> <div style="text-align: center;"><img alt="seasoned pretzel pieces in a bowl." class="attachment-post-thumbnail size-post-thumbnail wp-image-159134 wp-post-image" height="1800" src="https://sallysbakingaddiction.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/12/easy-seasoned-hard-pretzels.jpg" width="1200" /></div> <p>I've served these seasoned pretzels on repeat for over a decade because they're VERY easy and VERY crowd pleasing. Deliciously savory and crunchy—I say with confidence that you will not be able to stop snacking on these. Just read some of the reviews!</p> <p>The post <a href="https://sallysbakingaddiction.com/moms-seasoned-pretzels/">Easy Seasoned Pretzels</a> appeared first on <a href="https://sallysbakingaddiction.com">Sally's Baking</a>.</p></p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://sallysbakingaddiction.com/moms-seasoned-pretzels/" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9518"> <h2>#9518. This Vitamin Reduces Depression Symptoms By 50%</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://www.spring.org.uk/images/pill8-1.jpg" alt="This Vitamin Reduces Depression Symptoms By 50%" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>One vitamin reduced depression symptoms after a month, but the benefit depended on how participants felt at the start.</p> <p>One vitamin reduced depression symptoms after a month, but the benefit depended on how participants felt at the start.</p> <p>Taking a high dose of vitamin B6 for a month reduced depression symptoms in people already experiencing them.</p> <p>The vitamin helps the brain produce chemical messengers involved in mood regulation.</p> <p>The findings suggest a potential role for B6 in treating depression, although larger clinical trials are needed.</p> <p>Almost 270 adults, mostly young women, took part in the research.</p> <p>They were randomly assigned to take either 100 mg of vitamin B6, vitamin B12 or a placebo each day for around a month.</p> <p>Among almost 60 people with at least mild depression symptoms at the start, those taking B6 improved more than those receiving B12 or a placebo.</p> <p>Average depression scores fell by about 54 percent in the symptomatic B6 group, compared with 24 percent in the placebo group.</p> <p>The benefit remained after accounting for differences in how severe their symptoms had been at the start.</p> <p>The findings come from a new analysis of data collected in the same research programme that previously reported reduced anxiety after B6 supplementation.</p> <p>Vitamin B6 supports several processes involved in regulating mood.</p> <p>Dr David Field, the study’s first author, said:</p> <p>“Vitamin B6 plays a crucial role in the production of several chemical messengers in the brain, including serotonin and GABA, both of which are central to mood regulation.”</p> <p>GABA helps restrain nerve cell activity, contributing to the balance between excitation and inhibition in the brain.</p> <p>Increasing B6 availability could boost their production, potentially explaining the improvement in depression symptoms.</p> <p>Inflammation may also play a role, potentially affecting both depression and how the body uses B6.</p> <p>Vitamin B6 occurs naturally in foods including poultry, fish, chickpeas, bananas and fortified cereals.</p> <p>However, the trial tested a high supplement dose, rather than a change in everyday food intake.</p> <p>High doses of B6 can cause peripheral nerve damage, so the researchers say supplementation at these doses requires medical supervision.</p> <p>Larger trials now need to establish the most effective dose, monitor safety and determine whether B6 could help alongside existing depression treatments.</p> <p>The study was published in the journal Depression and Anxiety (Field et al., 2026).</p> <p>Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean</p> <p>Join the free PsyBlog mailing list. No spam, ever.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://www.spring.org.uk/2026/10/vitamin-depression-54.php" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9517"> <h2>#9517. Eight galleries artfully made from concrete</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://static-2026.dezeen.com/uploads/2026/10/anselm-kiefer-pavilion-david-chipperfield-architects_dezeen_2364_hero_1.jpg" alt="Eight galleries artfully made from concrete" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Our latest roundup collects galleries where exposed concrete surfaces form contemplative settings for paintings and artwork.</p> <p>From high-profile art museums to modest pavilions housing singular artworks, the galleries below illustrate the endless and artful possibilities of concrete.</p> <p>Among the projects included in the roundup are buildings by Pritzker Prize-winning architects Peter Zumthor, Eduardo Souto de Moura, Tadao Ando and David Chipperfield Architects.</p> <p>Read on to discover eight concrete art galleries from around the world:</p> <p>The David Geffen Galleries, USA, by Peter Zumthor</p> <p>Wrapped in a ribbon of glazing, The David Geffen Galleries is a curving concrete extension to the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, designed by Swiss architect Peter Zumthor.</p> <p>The elevated gallery snakes above street level and spans Wilshire Boulevard. It is supported by seven structural pavilions that are scattered unevenly along its footprint.</p> <p>Casa das Histórias Paula Rego, Portugal, by Eduardo Souto de Moura</p> <p>Two pyramid-like chimneys rise from Casa das Histórias Paula Rego in Cascais, Portugal, which was designed by Portuguese architect Eduardo Souto de Moura to house the works of artist Paula Rego.</p> <p>Enclosed by red-concrete walls, the interior was designed as a sequence of rooms tailored to different formats, from small lithographs to large-scale paintings.</p> <p>Xiao Feng Art Museum, China, by ZAO/standardarchitecture</p> <p>Chinese studio ZAO/standardarchitecture created an angular concrete building looping around a central courtyard for the Xiao Feng Art Museum in Hangzhou.</p> <p>Dedicated to the artist couple Xiao Feng and Song Ren, the gallery rises and falls to form openings that guide visitors under bridge-like elements to the courtyard.</p> <p>Japanese architect Tadao Ando designed a subterranean concrete dome to house a permanent installation by British sculptor Antony Gormley at Museum SAN in Wonju, South Korea.</p> <p>Spanning 25 metres in width, the cave-like space was topped by a central oculus that looms over the cast-iron sculptures.</p> <p>Nubuke Extended, Ghana, by Baerbel Mueller and Juergen Strohmayer</p> <p>Nubuke Extended is a one-room concrete gallery extension to the Nubuke Foundation in Ghana, which was raised above the ground to form a shaded events and gathering space below.</p> <p>Designed by architect Baerbel Mueller and architectural designer Juergen Strohmayer, the gallery’s interior features high ceilings and a mezzanine level.</p> <p>Richard Serra gallery, USA, by Thomas Phifer and Partners</p> <p>At the Glenstone Museum in Maryland, American architecture studio Thomas Phifer and Partners created a rectangular gallery for the artworks of sculptor Richard Serra.</p> <p>The building was made from cast-in-place structural concrete with doors made of stainless steel, and a series of skylights provides the only source of light inside.</p> <p>Anselm Kiefer Pavilion, Germany, by David Chipperfield Architects</p> <p>Six years after completing the Carmen Würth Forum museum in Germany, architecture firm David Chipperfield Architects returned to the site to add a monolithic concrete gallery built around a singular large-scale artwork.</p> <p>Once too big to exhibit at the museum, the Schwarze Flocken artwork by Anselm Kiefer now hangs on the wall of the Anselm Kiefer Pavilion, illuminated by rooflights.</p> <p>Ginkgo Gallery, China, by MORE Architecture</p> <p>Scooped concrete ceilings animate the Ginkgo Gallery in Jiaxing, which was designed by Dutch studio MORE Architecture as an antidote to China‘s boom of large-scale museums.</p> <p>Located on an island in a manmade lake, the museum’s board-marked concrete surfaces were arranged to create horizontal patterns across the walls and roofs.</p>
